7.X Deep Dive — Circuit Breaker States: CLOSED→OPEN→HALF-OPEN

The circuit breaker state machine is tested on every ICA exam. Here's exactly what happens at each transition:

🔌 CIRCUIT BREAKER STATE MACHINE
  CLOSED (Normal)                    OPEN (Ejected)
  ┌──────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────┐
  │ All requests      │  5 errors   │ ALL requests      │
  │ forwarded to      │────────────▶│ FAIL IMMEDIATELY  │
  │ upstream pods     │  in 10s     │ with 503          │
  │                   │             │ NO network call!  │
  └──────────────────┘              └────────┬─────────┘
         ▲                                  │ 60s passes
         │          ┌──────────────────┐    │ (baseEjectionTime)
         │          │ HALF-OPEN        │◀───┘
         │          │ 1 probe request  │
         │ success  │ allowed through  │─── failure ──▶ back to OPEN
         └──────────│                  │
                    └──────────────────┘
  Key: OPEN state saves thread pools — no connections attempted, instant 503
💡 maxEjectionPercent — The Blast Radius Control

Default is 100% — ALL pods can be ejected simultaneously = complete outage! Always set maxEjectionPercent: 50 to keep at least half the pods in the pool. Formula: max ejected = ceil(total_pods × maxEjectionPercent/100). With 3 pods and 50%: max 2 ejected, 1 always serves.

📝 Chapter 7 — ICA Practice Questions (Hands-On Lab Scenarios)

Q1
You have two versions of jobpost-api deployed (v1 and v2) with matching pod labels. Task: Write a complete DestinationRule that (a) defines subsets v1 and v2 using label selectors, (b) sets the load balancer to LEAST_CONN, and (c) applies to the host jobpost-api. Then verify the subsets are populated using istioctl proxy-config endpoint. Explain what happens if pod labels don't match the subset labels and how to debug with kubectl get pods --show-labels.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_CONN
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2

# Apply
kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-dr.yaml

# Verify subsets have endpoints
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/source-pod -n anihpj | grep jobpost-api
# ✅ Should show pod IPs for both v1 and v2 subsets
# Debug: Check pod labels match subset labels
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=jobpost-api --show-labels
# ✅ version=v1 → subset v1 has endpoints
# ❌ version=stable → subset v1 EMPTY (label mismatch!)
# Fix: kubectl patch deployment jobpost-api-v1 -n anihpj \
#   --type='json' -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/metadata/labels/version","value":"v1"}]'
Explanation

DestinationRule subsets are the foundation of canary deployments. The subset labels are ANDed with the Service selector to find endpoints. If no pods have matching labels → zero endpoints → 503 for all traffic to that subset. On the ICA exam, always verify: kubectl get pods --show-labels and istioctl proxy-config endpoint. The host must be the FQDN or short name — both work. LEAST_CONN is best for variable-duration requests (like job processing).

Q2
Your user-service has 3 replicas and keeps failing under load. Task: Write a DestinationRule with circuit breaker (outlierDetection) that ejects a host after 5 consecutive 5xx errors within a 15-second window, and keeps it ejected for 60 seconds. Set maxEjectionPercent: 33 so 2 replicas always remain. Then simulate a failure: write a VirtualService that injects 100% 500 errors. Explain the full CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN → CLOSED lifecycle with timing.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: user-service-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 15s
      baseEjectionTime: 60s
      maxEjectionPercent: 33    # Only 1 of 3 can be ejected
# Simulate failure with VirtualService fault injection
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: user-service-fault-test
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - user-service
  http:
  - fault:
      abort:
        httpStatus: 500
        percentage:
          value: 100
    route:
    - destination:
        host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local

Lifecycle: CLOSED (healthy, serving) → 5 consecutive 500s within 15s → OPEN (ejected for 60s, all requests get immediate 503) → after 60s → HALF-OPEN (one probe request) → success → CLOSED. maxEjectionPercent: 33 = only 1 host ejected (ceil(3 × 0.33) = 1), 2 hosts always serve traffic.

Explanation

Circuit breaker configuration is a DestinationRule responsibility. Key fields: consecutive5xxErrors (HTTP errors), consecutiveGatewayErrors (includes TCP connection failures), interval (default 10s — the evaluation window), baseEjectionTime (default 30s). maxEjectionPercent is the BLAST RADIUS control — without it, ALL hosts can be ejected simultaneously. On the ICA exam, always set maxEjectionPercent in production scenarios. The 3-state lifecycle (CLOSED→OPEN→HALF-OPEN→CLOSED) is fundamental.

Q3
Your jobpost-api needs sticky sessions — the same user's requests must always hit the same pod for cache warmth. Task: Write a DestinationRule that uses CONSISTENT_HASH load balancing based on the HTTP header x-user-id. Verify that the same header value routes to the same pod using multiple curl calls. Then explain when to use CONSISTENT_HASH vs LEAST_CONN vs ROUND_ROBIN vs RANDOM load balancing.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      consistentHash:
        httpHeaderName: x-user-id   # Hash on user ID for sticky sessions
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
# Verify: Same x-user-id → same pod every time
for i in $(seq 1 5); do
  kubectl exec deploy/source -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s -H "x-user-id: user42" http://jobpost-api/pod-name
done
# Should return the SAME pod name for all 5 requests
LB AlgorithmBest For
LEAST_CONNVariable-duration requests (job processing, ML inference)
ROUND_ROBINStateless, uniform-duration requests (REST APIs)
RANDOMVery high throughput, stateless (proxy for similar services)
CONSISTENT_HASHSticky sessions, cache affinity (user sessions, ML model serving)
PASSTHROUGHDon't load balance — forward to original destination (TCP proxy)
Explanation

CONSISTENT_HASH is the go-to for session affinity. Hash sources: httpHeaderName, httpCookie (with ttl), useSourceIp, or httpQueryParameterName. On the ICA exam, the question hints at the algorithm: "variable duration" = LEAST_CONN, "sticky" or "cache" = CONSISTENT_HASH, "default" = ROUND_ROBIN. Consistent hashing also minimizes redistribution when pods scale — only ~1/N keys move when a pod is added/removed.

Q4
Your production cluster uses mTLS. You need to configure the client side of the connection for calls to user-service. Task: Write a DestinationRule with trafficPolicy.tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL. Create a matching PeerAuthentication with mode: STRICT for the anihpj namespace. Verify mTLS is working using istioctl proxy-config endpoints to check if endpoints show TLS. Then explain what happens if: (a) DestinationRule says ISTIO_MUTUAL but PeerAuthentication is DISABLE, (b) DestinationRule says DISABLE but PeerAuthentication is STRICT.
Show Answer
Answer
# DestinationRule: Client side (outbound)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: user-service-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    tls:
      mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL   # Client Envoy initiates mTLS using SPIFFE certs
# PeerAuthentication: Server side (inbound)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: anihpj-mtls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT          # Server Envoy REQUIRES mTLS from all clients
# Verify: Check if endpoints show TLS
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/source-pod -n anihpj | grep user-service
# MTLS column should show "ISTIO_MUTUAL"

(a) DR ISTIO_MUTUAL + PA DISABLE: Client sends mTLS, server accepts plaintext too — WORKS (in PERMISSIVE mode) or fails with TLS error (in DISABLE with no TLS listener).

(b) DR DISABLE + PA STRICT: ❌ Client sends plaintext HTTP, server requires mTLS → TLS handshake failure → 503. CRITICAL misconfiguration.

Explanation

The TLS handshake is a CONTRACT between client and server. DestinationRule = client side (what the outbound Envoy sends). PeerAuthentication = server side (what the inbound Envoy requires). They must be compatible. Production best practice: DR = ISTIO_MUTUAL + PA = STRICT = full mesh-wide mTLS. On the ICA exam, when debugging 503s between mesh services, check DR and PA alignment FIRST. The migration path: PERMISSIVE (accepts both) → STRICT (requires mTLS) after all sidecars are deployed.

Q5
You need to prevent jobpost-api from overwhelming user-service with too many concurrent connections. Task: Write a DestinationRule with connection pool limits: max 100 HTTP/1.1 connections, max 50 pending requests, max 200 requests per connection. Explain the difference between connection pool (proactive) and circuit breaker (reactive). Then explain what happens when a request exceeds these limits — does it get a 503 or queued?
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: user-service-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100           # Max total TCP connections
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 50   # Max queued HTTP/1.1 requests
        http2MaxRequests: 200         # Max concurrent HTTP/2 streams
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 200 # Max requests per TCP connection

Connection Pool vs Circuit Breaker: Connection pool is PROACTIVE — limits capacity BEFORE problems occur (prevents overload). Circuit breaker is REACTIVE — ejects hosts AFTER errors are detected (prevents cascading failures). They complement each other: connection pool protects the TARGET, circuit breaker protects the CALLER.

What happens on overflow: When limits are exceeded, Envoy returns 503 Service Unavailable with "upstream overflow" — requests are NOT queued beyond http1MaxPendingRequests. The response is immediate.

Explanation

Connection pool settings are your first line of defense against overload. They prevent one caller from monopolizing a service. On the ICA exam: "preventing overload" or "limiting concurrent requests" = connection pool (DestinationRule > trafficPolicy > connectionPool). "handling failures" or "ejecting broken hosts" = circuit breaker (DestinationRule > trafficPolicy > outlierDetection). Both are in the same DestinationRule but serve different purposes. For HTTP/2 (gRPC), use http2MaxRequests instead of http1MaxPendingRequests.

Q6
Circuit breaker ejected ALL 3 replicas of user-service — now every request gets 503. Task: Explain what went wrong (missing maxEjectionPercent). Fix the DestinationRule by adding maxEjectionPercent: 50. Then write a minHealthPercent configuration ensuring at least 50% of endpoints must be healthy. Explain how maxEjectionPercent and minHealthPercent work together to prevent total outages.
Show Answer
Answer
# FIXED DestinationRule with blast radius controls
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: user-service-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50      # Never eject > 50% of hosts (2 of 3 in pool)
      minHealthPercent: 50        # At least 50% must be healthy

maxEjectionPercent: Caps the circuit breaker's blast radius. Formula: max ejected = ceil(total_hosts × maxEjectionPercent / 100). With 3 hosts and 50%: max 2 ejected (ceil(3×0.5)=2). At least 1 stays in the pool.

minHealthPercent: If fewer than 50% of hosts are healthy (not ejected AND passing health checks), Envoy considers the entire cluster degraded and may apply different logic. Together they form a safety net against total outage.

Explanation

Without maxEjectionPercent, the default is 100% — ALL hosts can be ejected. A brief network blip affecting all replicas triggers circuit breakers on ALL of them simultaneously → complete outage. On the ICA exam, ALWAYS set maxEjectionPercent to something below 100% in production scenarios. The formula: if you have N replicas, set maxEjectionPercent to ((N-1)/N × 100) to ensure at least 1 replica always stays in the pool. For 3 replicas → 66% max.

Q7
You need different circuit breaker settings for v1 (stable) and v2 (canary) of jobpost-api. Task: Write a DestinationRule with per-subset trafficPolicy overrides: v1 gets conservative circuit breaker (eject after 10 errors), v2 gets aggressive (eject after 2 errors — it's experimental). Use trafficPolicy at the top level for shared settings (LEAST_CONN load balancing) and override only what differs in subsets. Explain the inheritance model of trafficPolicy.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:                  # SHARED: applies to all subsets
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_CONN
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
    trafficPolicy:                # OVERRIDE: v1-specific
      outlierDetection:
        consecutive5xxErrors: 10  # Conservative — v1 is stable
        baseEjectionTime: 30s
        maxEjectionPercent: 50
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
    trafficPolicy:                # OVERRIDE: v2-specific
      outlierDetection:
        consecutive5xxErrors: 2   # Aggressive — v2 is experimental
        baseEjectionTime: 60s
        maxEjectionPercent: 100

Inheritance model: Top-level trafficPolicy is the DEFAULT. Subset-level trafficPolicy MERGES with and OVERRIDES the top-level. v1 and v2 both get LEAST_CONN (inherited), but different outlierDetection (overridden). If a field is omitted at subset level, the top-level value applies.

Explanation

Per-subset overrides are essential for canary deployments where the canary needs tighter monitoring (aggressive circuit breaker) than the stable version. The inheritance model: top-level → subset level (merge+override). Top-level sets defaults, subsets override specifics. This avoids duplicating shared config (like loadBalancer) across every subset. On the ICA exam, use this pattern when different versions need different resilience settings.

Q8
Your mesh services need different load balancing for different call patterns. Task: Write THREE DestinationRules for anihpj: (a) jobpost-api uses LEAST_CONN (variable job processing times), (b) user-service uses CONSISTENT_HASH on x-session-id header (sticky sessions), (c) skills-service uses ROUND_ROBIN (stateless, uniform). Apply all three and verify using istioctl proxy-config cluster that each destination shows the correct LB algorithm. Explain which Envoy resource (cluster) holds the LB config.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) jobpost-api — LEAST_CONN for variable processing
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_CONN
# (b) user-service — CONSISTENT_HASH for sticky sessions
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: user-service-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      consistentHash:
        httpHeaderName: x-session-id
# (c) skills-service — ROUND_ROBIN for stateless uniform
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: skills-service-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: skills-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      simple: ROUND_ROBIN
# Verify LB config in Envoy clusters
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep -E "jobpost-api|user-service|skills-service"
# Each cluster shows LbPolicy in its JSON output

Where LB config lives: In Envoy's CLUSTER resource (istioctl proxy-config cluster). Each upstream service is a separate cluster in Envoy, and the DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.loadBalancer becomes the cluster's LbPolicy.

Explanation

Each service gets its own DestinationRule with the appropriate LB algorithm. On the ICA exam, match the algorithm to the workload: variable duration → LEAST_CONN, sticky sessions → CONSISTENT_HASH, stateless → ROUND_ROBIN. The Envoy cluster is the abstraction that holds the LB configuration — DestinationRule CRD → Istiod conversion → Envoy cluster config. Verify with istioctl proxy-config cluster — look for LbPolicy in the output.

Q9
You need a circuit breaker that handles BOTH HTTP 5xx errors AND TCP connection failures. Task: Write a DestinationRule using consecutiveGatewayErrors (which covers both) instead of consecutive5xxErrors. Explain the difference: what errors does each field catch? Set the interval to 10s, baseEjectionTime to 30s, and maxEjectionPercent to 50. Then explain when to use consecutiveLocalOriginFailures (for aggressive ejection of local callers).
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: user-service-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    outlierDetection:
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5     # HTTP 5xx + TCP connection failures
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
FieldCatchesUse Case
consecutive5xxErrorsHTTP 500, 502, 503, 504 responsesApplication-level failures
consecutiveGatewayErrors502, 503, 504 + TCP connection failuresBroader detection (default in production)
consecutiveLocalOriginFailuresLocal Envoy failures (timeout, reset)Aggressive — ejects on ANY local failure
Explanation

consecutiveGatewayErrors is the recommended production choice — it catches BOTH application failures (5xx) and infrastructure failures (TCP connect failures). consecutive5xxErrors only fires on HTTP response codes — a TCP connection refused with no response won't trigger it. On the ICA exam, when the scenario mentions "connection failures" or "network issues", use consecutiveGatewayErrors. When it mentions only "application errors", consecutive5xxErrors is acceptable.

Q10
You applied a VirtualService with weighted routing (90/10 to v1/v2) and a DestinationRule defining both subsets. Traffic to v2 gets 503. Task: Debug systematically: (a) check istioctl proxy-config endpoint to see if v2 subset has endpoints, (b) check pod labels with kubectl get pods --show-labels, (c) check istioctl proxy-status for sync issues, (d) verify the DestinationRule host name matches the Service FQDN exactly. Write the fix for each failure. Then explain the full chain from VirtualService → DestinationRule → Service → Endpoints.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Check v2 subset has endpoints
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep -A2 "v2"
# ❌ Empty → v2 subset resolves to zero pods

# (b) Check pod labels
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=jobpost-api --show-labels
# ❌ version=stable (not v2!) → no pods match subset label

# Fix: Update Deployment labels
kubectl patch deployment jobpost-api-v2 -n anihpj --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/metadata/labels/version","value":"v2"}]'

# (c) Check proxy sync
istioctl proxy-status
# All must show SYNCED

# (d) Verify host name match
kubectl get destinationrule jobpost-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep host:
# host: jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
kubectl get svc jobpost-api -n anihpj
# Service name must match

The full chain: VirtualService (decides subset v2) → DestinationRule (v2 = labels {version: v2}) → Service selector (app: jobpost-api) → Endpoints (pods matching app=jobpost-api AND version=v2). Break any link = 503.

Explanation

This is the most common canary deployment debugging scenario on the ICA exam. The 4-step chain: VirtualService → DestinationRule → Service → Endpoints. The most common failure: pod labels don't match subset labels. Second most common: DestinationRule host name doesn't match Service name. Always debug in this order: proxy-config endpoint first (tells you if Envoy knows about the pod), then pod labels (tells you if the label exists), then proxy-status (tells you if config is synced), then host name (tells you if DR is for the right service).

Chapter 8: ServiceEntry — Connecting to External Services

By default, Istio (in REGISTRY_ONLY mode) blocks ALL external traffic. Your anihpj app needs to call Stripe for payments, SendGrid for emails, and S3 for file uploads. ServiceEntry registers these external services so Istio knows about them — and can apply policies to them.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🌍 External 🎯 ICA 30%
🎓 ICA Relevance
Traffic Management 30%
💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 8
  • "Register external API" = ServiceEntry with hosts:, location: MESH_EXTERNAL, resolution: DNS
  • "No ServiceEntry in REGISTRY_ONLY" = 502 Bad Gateway — external calls BLOCKED
  • "Apply policies to external" = Once registered, create VirtualService/DestinationRule targeting the ServiceEntry host
  • "Switch to REGISTRY_ONLY" = Create ServiceEntries FIRST, then switch mode — never switch first
  • "Egress Gateway" = Central exit point — single source IP, central audit, PCI compliance
  • "Wildcards" = hosts: ["*.amazonaws.com"] — register entire domains
  • Exam hands-on: Write ServiceEntry YAML from scratch + attach VirtualService timeout

8.1 The Problem: Calling External APIs from Within the Mesh

🌍 ISTIO OUTBOUND TRAFFIC MODES
ALLOW_ANY

All external traffic passes uncontrolled. No policies.

REGISTRY_ONLY

Only registered ServiceEntry hosts allowed. Recommended for production.

Egress Gateway

All external traffic through one Pod. Central audit.

8.2 ServiceEntry YAML — Registering External Services

yaml — ServiceEntry for anihpj external services 

# Stripe payments API
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe-payments
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL       # tells Istio this is external
  resolution: DNS
---
# SendGrid email API
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: sendgrid-email
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.sendgrid.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
---
# AWS S3 (wildcard for all regions)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: aws-s3
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - "*.amazonaws.com"           # wildcard
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL

8.3 Egress Gateway — Controlled Exit from the Mesh

🔀 EGRESS GATEWAY — Centralized Outbound Traffic
❌ WITHOUT

jobpost-api → direct → api.stripe.com
user-service → direct → api.stripe.com
3 different source IPs, no audit

✅ WITH Egress Gateway

All Pods → egressgateway → external
✅ One fixed source IP
✅ Central audit log
✅ Block all by stopping gateway

8.X External Service Security Patterns — Production Best Practices

🛡️
Pattern 1: Whitelist-Only

Switch to REGISTRY_ONLY mode. Create ServiceEntries ONLY for APIs you need. All other external traffic is blocked by default. This is zero-trust for egress.

istioctl install --set meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode=REGISTRY_ONLY -y
🚪
Pattern 2: Egress Gateway

Route ALL external traffic through a single egress gateway pod. Single source IP for firewall rules. Central audit. Block all egress by stopping one pod.

Gateway(type:egress) → VirtualService → ServiceEntry
🔄 EXTERNAL TRAFFIC POLICY DECISION — Which Mode for Production?
Production security requirements?
Basic: allow everything
→ ALLOW_ANY (default, NOT recommended)
Standard: whitelist-only
→ REGISTRY_ONLY + ServiceEntries
✅ Recommended for most production
Strict: full audit + single IP
→ REGISTRY_ONLY + Egress Gateway
✅ Required for PCI/HIPAA compliance

8.X Deep Dive — Egress Gateway Traffic Path Step-by-Step

When you configure an Egress Gateway, traffic takes a specific 4-hop path. Understanding this flow is critical for the ICA exam:

🔀 EGRESS GATEWAY TRAFFIC FLOW — 4 Hops to the Internet
HOP 1: Pod → Sidecar Envoy (outbound :15001)
  App calls api.stripe.com:443 → iptables redirects to Envoy :15001
  Envoy matches VirtualService: "route to egress gateway"
  
HOP 2: Sidecar Envoy → istio-egressgateway Pod
  Traffic forwarded to istio-egressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local:443
  mTLS between sidecar and egress gateway (SPIFFE certs)
  
HOP 3: Egress Gateway → External API (api.stripe.com)
  Gateway matches its own VS rules: "route to api.stripe.com"
  Performs DNS resolution, establishes TLS to Stripe
  
HOP 4: Response flows back through same path
  Stripe → Egress Gateway → Sidecar Envoy → App container
  Headers, status codes, body — all proxied transparently
💡 Why Egress Gateway Matters

Single source IP: Stripe sees all requests from ONE IP (the egress gateway Node IP) — simpler firewall rules. Central audit: All external calls logged in ONE place. Kill switch: Stop the egress gateway pod = ALL external traffic blocked instantly. Required for PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC2 compliance.

8.Y Deep Dive — DNS Proxying & Protocol Selection: How Istio Routes Without HTTP Headers

Two critical operational features from the official docs that every ICA candidate must understand:

🌐 DNS Proxying — ServiceEntry Resolution Without Custom DNS

By default, Kubernetes DNS doesn't know about ServiceEntry hosts. DNS Proxying makes the Envoy sidecar intercept DNS queries from the application and resolve ServiceEntry addresses locally — no external DNS changes needed.

  WITHOUT DNS Proxying:
  App → DNS query: "api.stripe.com" → kube-dns → ❌ NXDOMAIN (unknown)
  
  WITH DNS Proxying:
  App → DNS query: "api.stripe.com" → Sidecar intercepts → Checks ServiceEntry registry
  → Returns: 240.240.0.1 (auto-allocated VIP) → App sends request to VIP
  → Envoy routes VIP → ServiceEntry → api.stripe.com:443
# Enable DNS Proxying (sidecar mode)
apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: IstioOperator
spec:
  meshConfig:
    defaultConfig:
      proxyMetadata:
        ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE: "true"  # Enable DNS interception
# Or per-pod annotation:
# proxy.istio.io/config: proxyMetadata.ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE: "true"
# Ambient mode: enabled by default from Istio 1.25+
💡 Address Auto-Allocation

For ServiceEntries without explicit spec.addresses, Istio auto-allocates VIPs from the 240.240.0.0/16 range (Class E, non-routable). Each ServiceEntry gets a unique VIP. Envoy routes based on this VIP to distinguish multiple TCP services on the same port. Opt-out: networking.istio.io/enable-autoallocate-ip: "false" label on ServiceEntry.

🔌 Protocol Selection — How Istio Knows HTTP vs TCP

Istio can proxy ANY TCP traffic, but L7 features (routing, metrics, retries) require protocol identification. Two methods:

MethodHowExamplePriority
appProtocol (K8s 1.18+)Service port fieldappProtocol: https🥇 HIGHEST
Port namename: <protocol>[-suffix]name: http-web or grpc-api🥈 Second
Auto-detectionEnvoy inspects trafficDetects HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2🥉 Fallback (→ TCP if unknown)
kind: Service
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 443
    name: https-api      # ← Protocol detected: HTTPS
    appProtocol: https   # ← Explicit (takes precedence)
  - port: 9090
    name: grpc-metrics   # ← Protocol detected: gRPC (HTTP/2)
  - port: 5432
    name: tcp-postgres   # ← Protocol detected: TCP
⚠️ ICA: Port Name is MANDATORY for L7 Features

If a port is named myapp-port instead of http-myapp, Istio treats it as opaque TCP — no VirtualService routing, no metrics labels, no retries. The protocol prefix in the port name is NOT optional for L7 features. Supported prefixes: http, http2, grpc, grpc-web, tcp, tls, https. Also: gateways don't auto-detect HTTP protocol — they default to HTTP/1.1 unless explicitly set.

📝 Chapter 8 — ICA Practice Questions (Hands-On Lab Scenarios)

Q1
Your jobpost-api needs to call Stripe's payment API at api.stripe.com on port 443. Currently the cluster uses REGISTRY_ONLY mode and all external calls fail with 502. Task: Write a ServiceEntry to register Stripe. Verify the entry is working by curling api.stripe.com from inside a pod. Then write a DestinationRule that enforces SIMPLE TLS on port 443 for Stripe calls. Explain the full flow: ServiceEntry → Istio registry → Envoy cluster → external connection.
Show Answer
Answer
# ServiceEntry: Register Stripe in Istio's registry
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe-payments
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
# DestinationRule: Enforce TLS for Stripe calls
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: stripe-tls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: api.stripe.com
  trafficPolicy:
    tls:
      mode: SIMPLE    # One-way TLS — Stripe presents certificate
# Verify: curl from inside a pod
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- \
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://api.stripe.com
# ✅ Returns 200 (or 401 — Stripe requires auth, but TLS works)

# Check Envoy cluster was created
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep stripe
# ✅ Shows outbound cluster for api.stripe.com:443

Flow: ServiceEntry → Istiod adds host to service registry → Istiod pushes cluster config to Envoy → DestinationRule adds TLS policy → Envoy initiates HTTPS connection to Stripe.

Explanation

ServiceEntry brings external APIs into Istio's service registry. Without it (in REGISTRY_ONLY mode), the Envoy sidecar has no cluster for api.stripe.com — requests fail with 502. On the ICA exam, the pattern is always: ServiceEntry (register) → optional DestinationRule (TLS/policy) → optional VirtualService (retries/timeouts). ServiceEntry enables full Istio policy control over external traffic — retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, fault injection ALL work for external APIs once registered.

Q2
Your production security audit requires that ALL external traffic be explicitly allowed — no implicit passthrough. Task: (a) Switch the mesh from ALLOW_ANY to REGISTRY_ONLY mode, (b) FIRST create ServiceEntries for three external APIs that anihpj uses: Stripe (api.stripe.com:443), SendGrid (api.sendgrid.com:443), and AWS S3 (s3.amazonaws.com:443). (c) Explain the CORRECT migration sequence and what happens if you reverse the order. Write the command to verify the current outbound mode.
Show Answer
Answer
# STEP 1: Create ServiceEntries FIRST (before switching mode)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts: [api.stripe.com]
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: sendgrid
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts: [api.sendgrid.com]
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: aws-s3
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts: ["s3.amazonaws.com", "*.s3.amazonaws.com"]
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
# STEP 2: Switch to REGISTRY_ONLY mode
istioctl install --set meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode=REGISTRY_ONLY -y

# STEP 3: Verify current mode
kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A2 outboundTrafficPolicy
# mode: REGISTRY_ONLY ✅

# STEP 4: Test each external API still works
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -sk https://api.stripe.com

Wrong order = outage: If you switch to REGISTRY_ONLY FIRST, ALL external calls immediately fail with 502. The ServiceEntries created AFTER switching won't help the ongoing failures — they only work going forward. Always create entries FIRST, then switch.

Explanation

This is a critical operational sequence tested on the ICA exam. The migration is: audit → create ServiceEntries → test (with ALLOW_ANY) → switch to REGISTRY_ONLY → verify. Never reverse this order. ALLOW_ANY (demo default) = all external traffic allowed. REGISTRY_ONLY (production default) = only explicitly registered. The audit step is important — you need to know ALL external calls your services make BEFORE you can block them.

Q3
Your security team wants ALL external traffic from anihpj to exit through a single point — the Egress Gateway — so they can audit and control it. Task: Write the complete 3-resource configuration: (a) Gateway (type egress), (b) VirtualService (routes Stripe traffic through the egress gateway), (c) ServiceEntry for api.stripe.com. The sidecar should NOT connect to Stripe directly — it must go through the egress gateway. Explain the traffic path: pod → sidecar → egress gateway → internet.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Gateway: Egress listener
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: istio-egressgateway
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  selector:
    istio: egressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
    hosts:
    - api.stripe.com
    tls:
      mode: PASSTHROUGH   # Don't terminate TLS — pass through to Stripe
# (b) ServiceEntry: Register Stripe
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
# (c) VirtualService: Route through egress gateway
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: stripe-through-egress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  gateways:
  - mesh                    # Applies to ALL sidecars in mesh
  - istio-system/istio-egressgateway
  http:
  - match:
    - gateways:
      - mesh                # Traffic from sidecar → egress gateway
      port: 443
    route:
    - destination:
        host: istio-egressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
        port:
          number: 443
  - match:                  # Traffic from egress gateway → internet
    - gateways:
      - istio-system/istio-egressgateway
      port: 443
    route:
    - destination:
        host: api.stripe.com

Traffic path: Pod → sidecar Envoy (matches VS, routes to egress) → istio-egressgateway pod (VS routes to api.stripe.com) → internet → Stripe.

Explanation

The Egress Gateway is the controlled exit point for all external traffic. Three resources are required: Gateway (defines the listener on egressgateway), ServiceEntry (registers the external host), VirtualService (redirects traffic through the egress gateway with two match blocks — one for mesh→gateway, one for gateway→internet). On the ICA exam, this is the most complex ServiceEntry scenario. Benefits: single source IP for firewall rules, centralized audit logging, ability to block all egress by stopping one pod.

Q4
You registered api.sendgrid.com with a ServiceEntry but calls fail intermittently because SendGrid uses multiple IP addresses behind DNS. Task: (a) Write a ServiceEntry with resolution: DNS (not STATIC). (b) Explain how DNS resolution works in the Envoy sidecar vs STATIC resolution. (c) Write a ServiceEntry using resolution: STATIC with explicit IPs for a service with fixed addresses. Explain when to use each resolution mode.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) DNS resolution — handles dynamic IPs
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: sendgrid
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.sendgrid.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS    # Envoy resolves hostname → IPs via DNS, refreshes periodically
# (c) STATIC resolution — for known fixed IPs
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: internal-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - db.internal.example.com
  addresses:
  - 10.0.1.50
  - 10.0.1.51
  ports:
  - number: 5432
    name: postgres
    protocol: TCP
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: STATIC   # Uses hardcoded IPs — no DNS lookup needed
ResolutionWhen to Use
DNSCloud APIs with dynamic DNS (Stripe, SendGrid, AWS) — 90% of cases
STATICInternal services with fixed IPs (VMs, legacy databases)
NONERouting already handled by network — Envoy does nothing
Explanation

For cloud APIs, always use DNS resolution. Envoy periodically re-resolves the hostname and updates its endpoint list — this handles CDN IP rotations and failover. STATIC is only for services where you KNOW the IPs won't change (internal databases on VMs). NONE is rarely used — it means "don't touch the routing, the network handles it." On the ICA exam, DNS resolution covers 90% of external service scenarios.

Q5
After registering Stripe with a ServiceEntry, jobpost-api calls to Stripe still get 502. Task: Debug systematically: (a) verify the ServiceEntry exists and is in the correct namespace, (b) verify outboundTrafficPolicy mode, (c) verify the Envoy cluster exists using istioctl proxy-config cluster, (d) check if a NetworkPolicy is blocking egress traffic, (e) verify DNS resolution from inside the pod. Write the command and expected output for each step. Fix the most likely cause.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Verify ServiceEntry exists in correct namespace
kubectl get serviceentry -n anihpj
# ✅ stripe-payments should be listed
# ❌ Not found → ServiceEntry in wrong namespace (must be same as calling pod)

# (b) Verify outbound mode
kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep outboundTrafficPolicy
# ALLOW_ANY ✅  |  REGISTRY_ONLY + no SE → 502 ❌

# (c) Verify Envoy cluster exists
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep stripe
# ✅ outbound|443||api.stripe.com — cluster exists
# ❌ Empty → ServiceEntry not synced or wrong namespace

# (d) Check NetworkPolicy
kubectl get networkpolicy -n anihpj
# Any DENY egress policy blocks external traffic

# (e) DNS resolution from pod
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- nslookup api.stripe.com
# ✅ Returns IP addresses
# ❌ No resolution → CoreDNS issue, not Istio

Most likely fix: ServiceEntry is in the wrong namespace. ServiceEntries are namespace-scoped — they only affect sidecars in the SAME namespace. Move the ServiceEntry to anihpj or create it there.

Explanation

ServiceEntry debugging on the ICA exam follows this checklist: exists? → right namespace? → mode allows it? → Envoy knows about it? → DNS resolves? → no network blocks? The most common mistake: creating the ServiceEntry in istio-system instead of the application namespace. ServiceEntries are namespace-scoped by default — they only work for pods in the same namespace. Use exportTo: ["*"] to make a ServiceEntry available mesh-wide.

Q6
You need to register ALL AWS S3 endpoints — the main API and all regional endpoints. Task: Write a single ServiceEntry that covers s3.amazonaws.com and ALL regional subdomains like s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. Use wildcard hosts. Also register the AWS STS endpoint sts.amazonaws.com in the SAME ServiceEntry. Explain the wildcard support in ServiceEntry hosts and its limitations (single-level only).
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: aws-services
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - "s3.amazonaws.com"
  - "*.s3.amazonaws.com"          # Matches s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, etc.
  - "sts.amazonaws.com"
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS

Wildcard limitations: *.s3.amazonaws.com matches s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com (single level) but NOT s3.us-east-1.s3.amazonaws.com (double level — no double wildcard support). For multi-level subdomains, list them explicitly or use separate ServiceEntries.

Explanation

Wildcards in ServiceEntry hosts follow DNS wildcard rules: * matches exactly one DNS label. *.example.com matches foo.example.com but NOT foo.bar.example.com. On the ICA exam, when registering services with multiple regional endpoints (AWS, GCP), use wildcards. You can list multiple hosts in one ServiceEntry — put the wildcard alongside explicit hostnames. This keeps your configuration DRY.

Q7
After registering Stripe, you want to add resilience: Task: Write a VirtualService for api.stripe.com with (a) 5s timeout, (b) 2 retries on 5xx with 1s perTryTimeout, (c) verify the budget fits. Then write a DestinationRule with circuit breaker: eject after 5 consecutive 5xx errors. Explain why you can apply VirtualService and DestinationRule to external services just like internal ones — because ServiceEntry made them mesh citizens.
Show Answer
Answer
# VirtualService: Timeout + Retries for Stripe
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: stripe-resilience
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  http:
  - timeout: 5s
    retries:
      attempts: 2
      perTryTimeout: 1s
      retryOn: 5xx
    route:
    - destination:
        host: api.stripe.com
# Budget: (2 retries × 1s) + 1s first attempt = 3s ≤ 5s ✅
# DestinationRule: Circuit breaker for Stripe
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: stripe-cb
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: api.stripe.com
  trafficPolicy:
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 60s
      maxEjectionPercent: 100

Why this works: ServiceEntry added api.stripe.com to Istio's service registry. From Istio's perspective, it's now indistinguishable from an internal service. VirtualService and DestinationRule work identically — you use the hostname as the key, and Envoy applies the policies to the outbound cluster.

Explanation

ServiceEntry makes external APIs first-class mesh citizens. Once registered, you get the FULL Istio policy surface: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, fault injection, connection pools, and traffic splitting. On the ICA exam, this is a key concept — the question may ask "can you apply a circuit breaker to an external API?" The answer is YES, but ONLY after creating a ServiceEntry. Without it, the host doesn't exist in Envoy's cluster table.

Q8
You created a ServiceEntry for api.stripe.com in namespace anihpj, but services in istio-system also need to call Stripe and they get 502. Task: Explain why namespace-scoped ServiceEntries don't work across namespaces by default. Fix it by adding exportTo: ["*"] to make it mesh-wide. Then explain the alternative approach of creating a separate ServiceEntry in istio-system. Which is better for an ICA exam scenario where only one namespace needs external access?
Show Answer
Answer
# FIX: Make ServiceEntry mesh-wide
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe-payments
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  exportTo:
  - "*"                    # Available to ALL namespaces in the mesh
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
# Alternative: Create in istio-system (also visible mesh-wide)
# ServiceEntries in istio-system are visible to all namespaces by default

ICA exam choice: If only anihpj needs external access → keep it namespaced (no exportTo). If multiple namespaces need it → add exportTo: ["*"] or move it to istio-system. Least privilege principle: only export where needed.

Explanation

ServiceEntry visibility is controlled by exportTo. Default (no exportTo) = visible only in the same namespace. exportTo: ["*"] = visible in ALL namespaces. exportTo: ["anihpj", "istio-system"] = visible in specific namespaces only. ServiceEntries in istio-system are auto-exported mesh-wide. On the ICA exam, when a ServiceEntry doesn't work from another namespace, check exportTo. The least-privilege approach: only export to namespaces that actually need it.

Q9
You need to register an on-prem VM running PostgreSQL at IP 10.0.1.50:5432 as part of the mesh. Unlike cloud APIs, this VM should get mTLS and be treated as a mesh-internal service. Task: Write a ServiceEntry with location: MESH_INTERNAL and resolution: STATIC. Also write a WorkloadEntry (if needed). Then write a DestinationRule with ISTIO_MUTUAL TLS mode for the PostgreSQL connection. Explain the difference between MESH_EXTERNAL (no mTLS) and MESH_INTERNAL (can enforce mTLS).
Show Answer
Answer
# ServiceEntry: Register VM as MESH_INTERNAL
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: postgres-vm
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - postgres.internal.example.com
  addresses:
  - 10.0.1.50
  ports:
  - number: 5432
    name: postgres
    protocol: TCP
  location: MESH_INTERNAL     # Part of the mesh — can enforce mTLS
  resolution: STATIC          # Fixed IP — no DNS needed
# DestinationRule: Enforce mTLS
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: postgres-mtls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: postgres.internal.example.com
  trafficPolicy:
    tls:
      mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL    # Full mesh mTLS to the VM

MESH_EXTERNAL vs MESH_INTERNAL: MESH_EXTERNAL = cloud APIs (Stripe, SendGrid) — outside trust domain, no SPIFFE identity, SIMPLE TLS only. MESH_INTERNAL = your VMs/bare metal — inside trust domain, can get SPIFFE identity, ISTIO_MUTUAL supported.

Explanation

MESH_INTERNAL is for services you OWN that run outside Kubernetes — VMs, bare metal, or other clusters. They're part of your trust domain and can participate in mTLS. MESH_EXTERNAL is for services you DON'T own — Stripe, AWS, SendGrid. On the ICA exam, the question hints: "on-prem VM" or "your database" = MESH_INTERNAL; "third-party API" or "cloud service" = MESH_EXTERNAL. MESH_INTERNAL supports full Istio policies including AuthorizationPolicy.

Q10
Comprehensive task: Anihpj needs to call 5 external services securely and reliably. Task: (a) Switch the cluster to REGISTRY_ONLY mode. (b) Create ServiceEntries for: Stripe (api.stripe.com:443 HTTPS), SendGrid (api.sendgrid.com:443 HTTPS), AWS S3 (*.amazonaws.com:443 HTTPS), a partner API (partner.example.com:8443 HTTPS with MUTUAL TLS), and an internal monitoring tool (monitor.internal:9090 TCP). (c) For each, specify the correct location, resolution, and protocol. (d) For the partner API, add a DestinationRule with MUTUAL TLS and the correct secret reference. (e) Verify all ServiceEntries are applied.
Show Answer
Answer
# Stripe — Cloud API
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata: {name: stripe, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  hosts: [api.stripe.com]
  ports:
  - {number: 443, name: https, protocol: HTTPS}
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
---
# SendGrid — Cloud API
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata: {name: sendgrid, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  hosts: [api.sendgrid.com]
  ports:
  - {number: 443, name: https, protocol: HTTPS}
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
---
# AWS — Wildcard for all regions
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata: {name: aws, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  hosts: ["*.amazonaws.com"]
  ports:
  - {number: 443, name: https, protocol: HTTPS}
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
---
# Partner API — MUTUAL TLS
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata: {name: partner, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  hosts: [partner.example.com]
  ports:
  - {number: 8443, name: https-mutual, protocol: HTTPS}
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
---
# Internal monitoring — TCP
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata: {name: monitor, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  hosts: [monitor.internal]
  addresses: [10.0.2.100]
  ports:
  - {number: 9090, name: prometheus, protocol: TCP}
  location: MESH_INTERNAL
  resolution: STATIC
# (d) Partner API DestinationRule with MUTUAL TLS
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata: {name: partner-mtls, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  host: partner.example.com
  trafficPolicy:
    tls:
      mode: MUTUAL
      clientCertificate: /etc/certs/partner-client.crt
      privateKey: /etc/certs/partner-client.key
      caCertificates: /etc/certs/partner-ca.crt
# (e) Verify
kubectl get serviceentry -n anihpj
# ✅ 5 ServiceEntries listed
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep -E "stripe|sendgrid|amazonaws|partner|monitor"
Explanation

This comprehensive task covers ALL ServiceEntry patterns on the ICA exam. Key decisions: cloud APIs = MESH_EXTERNAL + DNS, internal services = MESH_INTERNAL + STATIC, partner APIs = MESH_EXTERNAL + MUTUAL TLS (DestinationRule). For protocol: HTTPS for L7-capable APIs (enables retries/timeouts), TCP for raw connections. Wildcards handle regional endpoints. Always end with verification using istioctl proxy-config cluster.

📝 Part 5 Summary — Traffic Management (30% of ICA)

  • Gateway: External entry — hosts, ports, TLS. MUST pair with VirtualService.
  • VirtualService: WHERE to route — URI, headers, weights, retries, timeouts, faults.
  • DestinationRule: HOW to send — subsets, LB, circuit breaker, TLS mode, connection pool.
  • ServiceEntry: Register external APIs — Stripe, SendGrid, S3.
  • Canary Pattern: VS weights + DR subsets = gradual shift with instant rollback.

💼 Part 5 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Write Gateway YAML to accept external traffic into the mesh
  • Write VirtualService YAML for path-based and weight-based routing
  • Do canary deployments: deploy v2 → route 5% → monitor → ramp up
  • Roll back instantly by changing one YAML weight — no downtime
  • Add retries + timeouts to VS (no code changes!)
  • Configure circuit breakers via DR outlierDetection
  • Set up intelligent LB: LEAST_CONN for variable workloads, CONSISTENT_HASH for sticky sessions
  • Register external APIs (Stripe, SendGrid, S3) via ServiceEntry
  • Remember the pattern: VS = WHERE, DR = HOW, GW = WHO enters

📊 Part 6: Observability — See Everything in Your Mesh Chapters 9-11

Chapter 9: Metrics — Measuring Every Request

Istio gives you automatic observability — metrics, traces, and access logs for every request, with ZERO code changes. This chapter covers the three pillars of observability and how Istio makes them available without touching your Django code.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 📊 Observability 🎯 ICA 15%
🎓 ICA Relevance
Observability 15%

  • "Check RED metrics" = Grafana Istio Service Dashboard
  • "Find why a request is slow" = Jaeger distributed tracing
  • "See live topology" = Kiali service graph

9.1 The Observability Pillars: Metrics, Traces, Logs

Observability has three pillars that work together to give you a complete picture of your system. Istio provides Metrics and Traces automatically — zero code changes needed in your Django app.

9.5 Custom Metrics & Telemetry API

Beyond RED metrics, you can add custom dimensions and labels using Istio's Telemetry API — without touching application code.

yaml — Telemetry: Add custom metric dimensions 

apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-metrics
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  metrics:
  - providers:
    - name: prometheus
    overrides:
    - match:
        metric: REQUEST_COUNT
      tagOverrides:
        job_category:
          value: request.headers["x-job-category"]
        user_region:
          value: request.headers["x-user-region"]

9.6 Access Logs — Auditing Every Request

From the official docs: Istio can generate access logs for every request flowing through the mesh. Unlike metrics (aggregate data) and traces (sampled requests), access logs provide a full record of every single request — source, destination, latency, status, headers, and more.

📝 ISTIO ACCESS LOG — Anatomy of a Log Entry
[2026-06-02T09:31:27.360Z] "GET /api/jobs/123 HTTP/1.1" 200 - "-" 0 135 5 2 "-" 
"curl/7.60.0" "d209e46f-9ed5-9b61-bbdd-43e22662702a" 
"jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8000" 
"10.244.1.5:8000" 
inbound|8000|http|jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local - 

BREAKDOWN:
  Timestamp: 2026-06-02T09:31:27.360Z
  Method:    GET /api/jobs/123
  Protocol:  HTTP/1.1
  Status:    200 (success)
  Latency:   5ms (request) + 2ms (response) = 7ms total
  Bytes:     0 sent, 135 received
  Client:    curl/7.60.0
  Trace ID:  d209e46f-9ed5-9b61-bbdd-43e22662702a  ← links to Jaeger!
  Target:    jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8000
  Direction: inbound (receiving traffic)
  TLS:       mutual_tls (if mTLS enabled)
yaml — Telemetry API: Configure access logs 
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-access-logs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessLogging:
  - providers:
    - name: envoy
    # Optional: filter to only log errors
    # filter:
    #   expression: response.code >= 400
💡 Access Logs vs Metrics vs Traces — When to Use Each

Metrics: "What percentage of requests are failing?" (aggregate). Traces: "Why was THIS specific request slow?" (sampled). Access Logs: "What exactly happened at 9:31:27 AM?" (every request, full detail). Access logs are essential for security audits and debugging specific errors.

9.7 Control Plane Metrics — Monitoring istiod Health

From the official docs: Istio's control plane (istiod) also exports self-monitoring metrics. These are separate from service-level metrics — they tell you about Istio's own health, not your services' health.

🕹️ KEY CONTROL PLANE METRICS — What to Monitor

Metric CategoryWhat It Tells YouExample
xDS Push LatencyHow fast istiod pushes config to Envoypilot_xds_push_time
Config Sync StatusHow many proxies are SYNCED vs STALEpilot_proxy_convergence_time
CSR HandlingCertificate signing request ratespilot_total_xds_rejects
Memory/CPUistiod resource consumptionprocess_resident_memory_bytes
Connected ProxiesNumber of Envoy sidecars connectedpilot_xds gauge
Config RejectsInvalid CRDs rejected by Galleypilot_total_xds_rejects
📖 Proxy-Level vs Service-Level vs Control-Plane Metrics

Proxy-level: Raw Envoy stats (cluster health, connection errors, SSL errors). Service-level: Istio's standard metrics (istio_requests_total, istio_request_duration_ms). Control-plane: istiod's own health metrics. On the ICA exam, service-level metrics are the most commonly tested — they're what you see in Grafana dashboards.

9.X Deep Dive — Counters vs Gauges vs Histograms in PromQL

Istio emits 3 types of Prometheus metrics. Using the wrong PromQL function gives meaningless results:

📊 METRIC TYPES
COUNTER

Only increases. Use rate() or increase(). NEVER query raw — shows meaningless massive number.

GAUGE

Goes up/down. Query raw or avg_over_time(). Shows current state at scrape moment.

HISTOGRAM

Bucket counts. Use histogram_quantile() for p50/p95/p99 percentiles.

📝 Chapter 9 — ICA Practice Questions (Hands-On Lab Scenarios)

Q1
Your jobpost-api error rate spiked from 0.5% to 12%. Task: (a) Open Prometheus via istioctl dashboard prometheus. (b) Write a PromQL query that shows the error rate percentage for jobpost-api over the last 5 minutes. (c) Write a PromQL query for p99 latency. (d) Write a query that shows request rate (RPS) per second. (e) Explain RED metrics: Rate, Errors, Duration. Together, these three queries answer: is it getting traffic, is it failing, is it slow?
Show Answer
Answer
# (b) Error rate percentage
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
  destination_service="jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local",
  response_code=~"5.*"}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
  destination_service="jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"}[5m]))
* 100

# (c) p99 latency
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  rate(istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket{
    destination_service="jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"}[5m]))

# (d) Request rate (RPS)
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
  destination_service="jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"}[5m]))

RED: Rate = requests/sec (is it getting traffic?). Errors = % of 5xx (is it failing?). Duration = p95/p99 latency (is it slow?). These 3 queries diagnose any service health issue.

Explanation

RED metrics are the foundation of service observability. On the ICA exam, you need to write these PromQL queries from memory. Key patterns: rate() converts counters to per-second; histogram_quantile() calculates percentiles; sum() aggregates across pods. The destination_service label uses FQDN: svc.ns.svc.cluster.local. Filter by response_code=~"5.*" for server errors.

Q2
Prometheus suddenly stopped showing metrics for jobpost-api — the target shows "DOWN." Task: Debug systematically: (a) verify the sidecar is running (2/2), (b) verify port 15090 is accessible from Prometheus, (c) check Prometheus targets page for scrape status, (d) verify no NetworkPolicy blocks port 15090, (e) check istioctl proxy-status. Write the exact command for each check and the expected output when healthy.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Sidecar running?
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=jobpost-api
# ✅ READY: 2/2 (both app + istio-proxy)
# ❌ 1/1 → sidecar not injected

# (b) Port 15090 accessible from Prometheus pod?
kubectl exec deploy/prometheus -n istio-system -- \
  curl -s http://JOBPOST_POD_IP:15090/metrics | head -5
# ✅ Shows Prometheus metrics output
# ❌ Connection refused → port not open or NetworkPolicy blocked

# (c) Prometheus targets
kubectl port-forward svc/prometheus 9090:9090 -n istio-system
# Open http://localhost:9090/targets
# ✅ All istio targets show "UP" with green bar
# ❌ "DOWN" → check scrape config and network

# (d) NetworkPolicy blocking 15090?
kubectl get networkpolicy -n anihpj
kubectl describe networkpolicy -n anihpj
# Check for any DENY egress or ingress on port 15090

# (e) Proxy sync status
istioctl proxy-status
# ✅ SYNCED — istiod can reach the proxy
Explanation

Metrics debugging on the ICA exam follows this chain: sidecar up? → port open? → network unblocked? → Prometheus scraping? → config synced? Port 15090 is the key — it's Envoy's Prometheus metrics endpoint, separate from data plane ports 15001/15006. Common culprits: NetworkPolicy blocking 15090, sidecar not injected, istiod not synced. Always check in this order.

Q3
You need per-user metrics for billing — track how many requests each x-user-tier (free/pro/enterprise) makes. Task: Write a Telemetry resource that adds a custom tag user_tier extracted from the x-user-tier HTTP header to the REQUEST_COUNT metric. Apply it to the anihpj namespace. Verify the tag appears in Prometheus by querying istio_requests_total{user_tier="pro"}. Then write a Grafana panel showing request count grouped by user_tier.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-custom-metrics
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  metrics:
  - providers:
    - name: prometheus
    overrides:
    - match:
        metric: REQUEST_COUNT
      tagOverrides:
        user_tier:
          value: request.headers["x-user-tier"]
        job_category:
          value: request.headers["x-job-category"]
# Verify in Prometheus
istioctl dashboard prometheus
# Query: istio_requests_total{user_tier="pro"}
# ✅ Should return matching time series

# Grafana panel query (grouped by user_tier):
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service=~"jobpost-api.*"}[5m])) by (user_tier)
Explanation

The Telemetry API customizes Istio's metrics WITHOUT touching application code. On the ICA exam, this is the answer when asked about "custom metrics" or "adding dimensions." The tagOverrides extract values from request headers, making them available as Prometheus labels. Supported metrics: REQUEST_COUNT, REQUEST_DURATION, REQUEST_SIZE, RESPONSE_SIZE. The Telemetry resource is namespace-scoped — apply to istio-system for mesh-wide defaults.

Open Istio's 4 Grafana dashboards. Task: (a) Identify which dashboard to use for each scenario: checking if istiod is healthy, viewing total mesh traffic, debugging one specific service, comparing two deployments of the same service. (b) Open the Service Dashboard for jobpost-api and locate the RED metrics panel. (c) Write the command to forward Grafana to your local machine. (d) Explain WHERE the metrics come from (Envoy → Prometheus → Grafana, no app code needed).
Show Answer
Answer
DashboardUse For
Istio Control Planeistiod health, CPU, memory, pilot errors
Istio MeshGlobal overview — total RPS, global error rate
Istio ServicePer-service RED — pick one service, see its health
Istio WorkloadCompare v1 vs v2 deployments side by side
 
# (c) Forward Grafana to localhost:3000
istioctl dashboard grafana
# Or manual: kubectl port-forward svc/grafana 3000:3000 -n istio-system

(d) Data flow: Envoy sidecar (emits metrics on :15090/metrics) → Prometheus (scrapes every 15s) → Grafana (queries Prometheus via PromQL) → Dashboard displays. ZERO application instrumentation needed.

Explanation

On the ICA exam, know WHICH Grafana dashboard to use for each scenario. Mesh = helicopter view (all services). Service = magnifying glass (one service). Workload = canary comparison (v1 vs v2). Control Plane = istiod health. The Service Dashboard is your daily driver — it shows client/server RPS, success rate, and latency percentiles for any service you select from the dropdown.

Q5
You need to generate a load test to verify metrics are flowing. Task: Write a bash loop that sends 100 requests to jobpost-api from inside the mesh at ~10 req/s. Before the test, open Prometheus and Grafana dashboards. After the test, locate the traffic spike in: (a) Grafana Service Dashboard (RPS graph), (b) Prometheus query showing increased istio_requests_total, (c) Kiali service graph showing traffic edges. Explain which metrics are counters (monotonically increasing) vs gauges (instantaneous).
Show Answer
Answer
# Load test: 100 requests at ~10 req/s
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  kubectl exec deploy/source -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://jobpost-api/health
  sleep 0.1
done
echo "Done! Check Grafana/Prometheus."
# (b) Prometheus: See the traffic spike
rate(istio_requests_total{
  destination_service="jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"}[1m])
# ✅ Graph jumps from baseline to ~10 RPS during test

Counter vs Gauge: istio_requests_total is a COUNTER — it only increases (monotonically). Use rate() to convert to per-second. istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket is also a counter (histogram buckets). Active connections and queue sizes are GAUGES — they go up and down.

Explanation

Understanding metric types is critical for PromQL. Counters only increase — you must use rate() or increase() to make them meaningful. Gauges fluctuate. Histograms store bucket counts (also counters) and you use histogram_quantile() to extract percentiles. On the ICA exam, if you query a counter without rate(), you'll see a massive number that keeps growing — that's wrong.

Q6
The ICA exam terminal has Istio and Prometheus running. Task: Write a PromQL query that finds the TOP 5 services by request rate across the entire mesh in the last 5 minutes. Then write a query that finds services with an error rate above 5%. Explain how Prometheus service discovery finds Envoy sidecars automatically via pod annotations.
Show Answer
Answer
# Top 5 services by request rate
topk(5,
  sum(rate(istio_requests_total[5m])) by (destination_service)
)

# Services with error rate > 5%
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{response_code=~"5.*"}[5m])) by (destination_service)
/
sum(rate(istio_requests_total[5m])) by (destination_service)
> 0.05

Service discovery: Prometheus auto-discovers Envoy sidecars via Kubernetes pod annotations prometheus.io/scrape: "true" and prometheus.io/port: "15090". Istio adds these annotations to every pod with a sidecar. No manual target configuration needed.

Explanation

These are operational PromQL queries you might need on the ICA exam. topk(N, query) returns the top N results. The by (destination_service) clause groups results by service name. Prometheus service discovery means you never manually add scrape targets — Istio annotates every sidecar pod automatically. The annotations are added by the injection webhook at pod creation time.

Q7
You need to compare p50, p95, and p99 latency for jobpost-api in one PromQL query. Task: Write the three queries. Open them in Grafana and notice that p99 is 10× higher than p50 — what does this tell you? Explain the tail latency problem and how circuit breakers help. Also write the rate query to see if the high p99 correlates with a traffic spike.
Show Answer
Answer
# p50 (median)
histogram_quantile(0.50,
  rate(istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket{
    destination_service="jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"}[5m]))

# p95
histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)

# p99 (tail latency)
histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)

# Traffic correlation
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
  destination_service="jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"}[5m]))

p99 10× p50 = TAIL LATENCY PROBLEM: Most requests are fast (p50 is low), but a small percentage are VERY slow (p99 is high). Common causes: GC pauses, database lock contention, cold caches. Circuit breakers help by ejecting slow pods, preventing them from dragging down p99.

Explanation

Tail latency (p99 ≫ p50) is the #1 performance red flag. p99 = "99% of users experience at most this latency." If p99 is 1.2s while p50 is 120ms, 1% of users are having a terrible experience. On the ICA exam, correlate p99 with traffic: if both spike together → overload. If p99 spikes alone → GC or database issue. Circuit breaker with outlier detection is the Istio fix — eject slow pods and route traffic to fast ones.

Q8
You applied a Telemetry resource for custom metrics but the new tag doesn't appear in Prometheus. Task: Debug: (a) verify the Telemetry resource is in the correct namespace, (b) check istioctl analyze for config errors, (c) verify the header name exactly matches the request header, (d) send test traffic WITH the header, (e) query the specific metric with the new tag. Explain the ~30-second propagation delay from Telemetry CRD apply → istiod → Envoy → Prometheus scrape.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Verify Telemetry is in correct namespace
kubectl get telemetry -n anihpj
# ✅ anihpj-custom-metrics exists
# ❌ Wrong namespace → Telemetry only applies to its own namespace

# (b) Config validation
istioctl analyze -n anihpj
# ✅ No errors
# ❌ Shows invalid header reference → fix the header name

# (c) Verify header name case-sensitivity
# request.headers["x-user-tier"] — must match EXACTLY
# "X-User-Tier" ≠ "x-user-tier" — HTTP is case-insensitive but Envoy config isn't

# (d) Send test traffic WITH the header
kubectl exec deploy/source -n anihpj -- \
  curl -s -H "x-user-tier: pro" http://jobpost-api/health

# (e) Query after Prometheus scrape interval (~15s):
# Wait 30-60 seconds, then:
istio_requests_total{user_tier="pro"}

Propagation delay: Telemetry CRD → istiod (processes ~5s) → pushes to Envoy via xDS (~5s) → Envoy starts adding tags → Prometheus scrapes next cycle (~15s). Total: ~25-30 seconds before the tag appears.

Explanation

Telemetry resources have a propagation delay — don't expect instant results. On the ICA exam, if a custom tag doesn't appear: 1) check namespace (Telemetry is namespace-scoped), 2) check istioctl analyze for errors, 3) verify header name, 4) send traffic WITH the header, 5) wait 30+ seconds. The header name is case-sensitive in the Envoy config, even though HTTP headers are case-insensitive.

Q9
The ICA exam asks you to verify Prometheus is collecting data. Task: (a) Open Prometheus dashboard and query up{job="envoy-stats"} — explain what this returns. (b) Query scrape_duration_seconds to verify scrape timing. (c) Check if any targets are DOWN. (d) Query istio_requests_total and confirm data exists for the anihpj namespace. (e) Write a query that shows the number of active Envoy proxies being scraped — should match the number of pods with sidecars.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) All Envoy targets UP?
up{job="envoy-stats"}
# ✅ Returns 1 for every Envoy proxy being scraped
# ❌ Returns 0 → proxy down or unreachable on port 15090

# (b) Scrape timing
scrape_duration_seconds{job="envoy-stats"}
# Should be < 1s — if higher, metrics collection is slow

# (c) Down targets
up{job="envoy-stats"} == 0
# Shows any proxies Prometheus can't reach

# (d) Data exists for anihpj?
istio_requests_total{destination_service=~ ".*anihpj.*"}
# ✅ Returns time series → data flowing
# ❌ Empty → no traffic or metrics not being emitted

count(up{job="envoy-stats"} == 1)
# Should equal: kubectl get pods -A -l security.istio.io/tlsMode --no-headers | wc -l
Explanation

up is a special Prometheus metric that equals 1 when the scrape target is reachable, 0 when it's not. On the ICA exam, this is your first check: up{job="envoy-stats"} tells you how many Envoy proxies Prometheus can reach. The count should match your total sidecar count. If it doesn't, some proxies are unreachable — check port 15090, NetworkPolicies, and pod health.

Chapter 10: Distributed Tracing — Follow Any Request Across All Services

A single GET /jobs/ triggers 5+ service calls. Without tracing, you have no idea which service is the bottleneck. Jaeger distributed tracing shows every hop, every duration, in one Gantt chart.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔭 Tracing 🎯 ICA 15%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand Trace vs Span: Trace = entire journey, Span = one service call
  • ✅ Propagate B3 tracing headers (x-b3-traceid, x-b3-spanid, etc.) in Django code
  • ✅ Use Jaeger to find bottlenecks: sort by Longest Duration → widest bar = problem
  • ✅ Configure tracing sampling rate: 100% dev, 1% prod via Telemetry API
  • ✅ Force-sample specific requests with x-b3-flags: 1 for targeted debugging
  • ✅ Debug broken traces: isolated spans = missing header propagation
💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 10
  • "Why are traces broken?" = Missing B3 header propagation — forward x-b3-* headers in your code
  • "Find the bottleneck" = Jaeger → sort by Longest Duration → widest Gantt bar
  • "No traces appearing" = Check sampling rate (0%?), Jaeger collector running?, Envoy can reach port 14268?
  • Envoy does 80%: Auto-injects headers, creates spans, reports to Jaeger. You do 20%: forward headers.
  • Force trace: curl -H "x-b3-flags: 1" — overrides sampling percentage

10.1 What is Distributed Tracing?

🔍
Trace

The entire journey of ONE request across all services. Contains multiple spans linked by a Trace ID.

📏
Span

One unit of work — one service call. Has start time, duration, and parent-child relationships.

🔭 DISTRIBUTED TRACE — anihpj GET /jobs/ (342ms total)
Trace ID: 7f3e9a12b4c06d8e    Duration: 342ms

▶ jobpost-api (GET /jobs/)                                 0ms → 342ms
  ▶ user-service (GET /users/42/)                         12ms → 87ms
    ▶ auth-service (POST /validate-token/)               15ms → 45ms
  ▶ skills-service (GET /skills/?ids=1,2,3)               92ms → 287ms
    ← 195ms ← SLOW! This is the bottleneck ⚠️
  ▶ location-service (GET /locations/7/)                 295ms → 320ms

🔍 skills-service call took 195ms — investigate database query!

10.2 How Istio Enables Tracing (Almost Automatically)

Envoy automatically injects tracing headers into every request. Your Django code just needs to forward them between services.

python — Django header propagation (required!) 

# Add this to your Django views that call other services:
ISTIO_HEADERS = [
    'x-request-id',
    'x-b3-traceid',        # ← links all spans together
    'x-b3-spanid',
    'x-b3-parentspanid',
    'x-b3-sampled',
    'x-b3-flags',
]

def get_jobs(request):
    # Forward tracing headers to propagate trace context:
    headers = {
        h: request.META.get('HTTP_' + h.upper().replace('-', '_'))
        for h in ISTIO_HEADERS
        if request.META.get('HTTP_' + h.upper().replace('-', '_'))
    }
    users = requests.get('http://user-service/users/', headers=headers)
    skills = requests.get('http://skills-service/skills/', headers=headers)
    # ...
⚠️ CRITICAL — No Header Propagation = Broken Traces

If you don't forward the x-b3-* headers, each service call becomes a separate, disconnected trace. You won't see the full call chain — just isolated spans. This is the #1 tracing mistake.

10.3 Jaeger — Visualizing Traces

Jaeger is the default tracing backend. Open with istioctl dashboard jaeger. Key features: trace search, service dependency graph, latency histograms.

💡 How to Find Bottlenecks in Jaeger

1. Open Jaeger → Search → sort by Longest Duration. 2. Click the slowest trace. 3. Look at the Gantt chart — the widest bar is the bottleneck. 4. Click that span to see tags: HTTP method, URL, status code. 5. Cross-reference with logs at that timestamp.

10.4 Tracing Sampling Rate

Tracing every request adds overhead. Istio defaults to 1% sampling — trace 1 out of 100 requests.

🟢 Dev: 100%

Trace everything. Useful for debugging locally.

🟡 Prod: 1-5%

Enough for statistical analysis without overhead. 100% is too expensive in production.
