10.X Deep Dive — The B3 Header Propagation Contract

Envoy auto-creates spans and injects B3 headers, but YOUR code must forward them. Here's the exact division of responsibility:

🔗 B3 HEADERS — Envoy (80%) vs You (20%)
Envoy SIDECAR automatically:          YOUR DJANGO CODE must:
• Creates span context                • Extract x-b3-* from request.META
• Injects x-b3-traceid                 • Add them to EVERY outbound requests.get() call
• Injects x-b3-spanid                  • Without forwarding: NEW trace per call (BROKEN!)
• Injects x-b3-parentspanid           
• Reports spans to Jaeger              Result if you DON'T forward:
                                       Jaeger shows isolated spans, not a call chain
⚠️ The #1 Tracing Mistake

Isolated spans in Jaeger = missing header propagation. Fix: forward x-b3-traceid, x-b3-spanid, x-b3-parentspanid, x-b3-sampled, x-b3-flags on every outbound HTTP call.

📝 Chapter 10 — ICA Practice Questions (Hands-On Lab Scenarios)

Q1
Your Jaeger shows isolated, disconnected spans instead of a full call chain for GET /jobs/ → user-service → skills-service. Task: Diagnose the root cause (missing header propagation). Write the Django code that forwards the 5 B3 tracing headers from incoming requests to outbound HTTP calls. Apply the fix, generate a test request, and verify in Jaeger that ALL spans now share the same Trace ID. Explain which part is Istio's responsibility (span creation) and which part is yours (header propagation).
Show Answer
Answer
# Django header propagation — the MISSING piece
ISTIO_HEADERS = [
    'x-b3-traceid',
    'x-b3-spanid',
    'x-b3-parentspanid',
    'x-b3-sampled',
    'x-b3-flags',
]

def propagate_tracing_headers(request):
    """Extract B3 headers from incoming request for outbound calls."""
    headers = {}
    for header in ISTIO_HEADERS:
        # Django converts headers: x-b3-traceid → HTTP_X_B3_TRACEID
        django_key = 'HTTP_' + header.upper().replace('-', '_')
        value = request.META.get(django_key)
        if value:
            headers[header] = value
    return headers

# Usage in views:
def get_jobs(request):
    trace_headers = propagate_tracing_headers(request)
    users_resp = requests.get('http://user-service/users/',
                              headers=trace_headers)
    skills_resp = requests.get('http://skills-service/skills/',
                               headers=trace_headers)

Istio's part: Envoy CREATES the initial span context (generates Trace ID, Span ID) and injects headers into the first request. Envoy REPORTS spans to Jaeger.

Your part: FORWARD the headers between service calls. Without forwarding, each service creates a NEW trace instead of continuing the existing one.

Explanation

This is the #1 tracing issue on the ICA exam. Envoy does the heavy lifting: span creation, header injection, and reporting. But Envoy cannot automatically forward headers between YOUR application's outbound HTTP calls — that's your responsibility. The 80/20 rule: Istio = 80% (infrastructure), your code = 20% (header forwarding). The fix is always the same: extract B3 headers from the incoming request and add them to outbound calls.

Q2
The anihpj DevOps team wants 100% tracing in development but only 1% in production. Task: Write TWO Telemetry resources — one for the anihpj-dev namespace with 100% sampling, one for istio-system (mesh-wide default) with 1%. Explain the difference between randomSamplingPercentage and what happens at 0% vs 100%. Verify the setting took effect by checking a trace's x-b3-sampled header value.
Show Answer
Answer
# Development: 100% sampling (trace everything)
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: dev-tracing
  namespace: anihpj-dev
spec:
  tracing:
  - randomSamplingPercentage: 100.0

# Production: 1% mesh-wide default
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: mesh-default-tracing
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  tracing:
  - randomSamplingPercentage: 1.0
PercentageBehaviorUse Case
100%Every request traced — high overheadDevelopment, debugging
1-5%Statistical sampling — low overheadProduction
0%No traces — x-b3-sampled: 0 on all requestsDisable tracing completely
Explanation

The Telemetry API is the modern way to configure tracing sampling. Apply to istio-system for mesh-wide defaults, or to specific namespaces for overrides. The sampling decision is made by Envoy at request time — when x-b3-sampled: 0, the trace is NOT reported to Jaeger (saving CPU and storage). On the ICA exam, the Telemetry resource is the correct answer for sampling configuration — not the old meshConfig approach.

Q3
You're given a Jaeger trace showing 5 spans for GET /jobs/123. Task: (a) Identify which span is the bottleneck by looking at duration bars. (b) Click the slowest span and read its tags — what HTTP method, URL, and status code are shown? (c) Explain what Trace ID, Span ID, and Parent Span ID tell you about the request hierarchy. (d) Draw the call tree: jobpost-api → user-service → auth-service, jobpost-api → skills-service, jobpost-api → location-service. Which span has NO parent?
Show Answer
Answer

(a) Bottleneck: The WIDEST horizontal bar in the Gantt chart = slowest span. Click it to see duration and tags.

(b) Tags on the slowest span: http.method: GET, http.url: /skills/?ids=1,2,3, http.status_code: 200, component: proxy.

(c) Three IDs: Trace ID = same for ALL spans (journey-level). Span ID = unique per span (step-level). Parent Span ID = who called this span (creates the tree).

(d) Call tree with no parent:

Trace ID: 7f3e9a12b4c06d8e
├─ jobpost-api (GET /jobs/123/)          ← ROOT SPAN (no parent)
│  ├─ user-service (GET /users/42/)      ← parent: jobpost-api
│  │  └─ auth-service (POST /validate/)  ← parent: user-service
│  ├─ skills-service (GET /skills/)      ← parent: jobpost-api ← BOTTLENECK (195ms)
│  └─ location-service (GET /locations/) ← parent: jobpost-api
Explanation

The root span (first service that received the request) has NO Parent Span ID. Every other span has a Parent Span ID pointing to the calling service. On the ICA exam, you'll read trace diagrams and identify: the root span (no parent), the bottleneck (widest bar), and the call hierarchy (parent-child relationships via Span IDs). The Gantt chart visualizes this: indented bars under their parent span.

Q4
Your Django application makes 3 downstream calls per request. You need to ensure traces propagate correctly. Task: Write a Django MIDDLEWARE (not per-view code) that automatically forwards all B3 headers on every outbound requests.get() call. Test by making a request and checking Jaeger shows all 4 spans (1 root + 3 children) sharing the same Trace ID. Explain why middleware is better than per-view header forwarding.
Show Answer
Answer
# middleware.py — Automatic tracing header propagation
class IstioTracingMiddleware:
    """Automatically forwards Istio B3 tracing headers on outbound requests."""
    
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response
    
    def __call__(self, request):
        # Store tracing headers on request for later use
        request.istio_trace_headers = {
            header: request.META.get(
                'HTTP_' + header.upper().replace('-', '_')
            )
            for header in [
                'x-b3-traceid', 'x-b3-spanid',
                'x-b3-parentspanid', 'x-b3-sampled', 'x-b3-flags'
            ]
            if request.META.get(
                'HTTP_' + header.upper().replace('-', '_')
            )
        }
        return self.get_response(request)

# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'anihpj.middleware.IstioTracingMiddleware',
    # ... other middleware
]

Why middleware: One place, all views covered, no code duplication, impossible to forget. Per-view forwarding requires every developer to remember — middleware is automatic and enforced.

Explanation

Middleware is the production-grade approach to tracing header propagation. It processes EVERY request automatically — no developer needs to add forwarding code to their views. On the ICA exam, if asked about "best practice" for Istio tracing, middleware is the answer. The pattern: extract headers once in middleware → store on request object → use in outbound calls.

Q5
Open Jaeger and find the SLOWEST trace in the last 15 minutes involving jobpost-api. Task: (a) Navigate Jaeger UI → Search → Service: jobpost-api → sort by Longest Duration. (b) Identify which span is the bottleneck. (c) Click the span and list ALL tags visible. (d) Explain how to correlate this trace with logs at the same timestamp. (e) If the bottleneck span is an external API call (Stripe), write the ServiceEntry + DestinationRule that adds a timeout and circuit breaker to prevent future slowdowns.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Jaeger search
# Open istioctl dashboard jaeger
# Service: jobpost-api.anihpj
# Operation: all
# Sort by: Longest Duration ↓
# Time range: Last 15 minutes

# (b-c) Click the slowest trace → widest bar = bottleneck span
# Tags: http.method, http.url, http.status_code, component, upstream_cluster
# (e) If Stripe is the bottleneck:
# ServiceEntry (already exists)
# DestinationRule with circuit breaker
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: stripe-resilience
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: api.stripe.com
  trafficPolicy:
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 3
      baseEjectionTime: 60s
      maxEjectionPercent: 100

# VirtualService with timeout
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: stripe-timeout
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  http:
  - timeout: 3s
    route:
    - destination:
        host: api.stripe.com
Explanation

This is an end-to-end performance debugging workflow for the ICA exam. Find the slow trace → identify the bottleneck span → read span tags → correlate with logs → apply fix (timeout/circuit breaker). The key insight: Jaeger shows you WHICH service call is slow; you then use the span's timestamp to find related logs. External API calls are common bottlenecks — always add timeouts and circuit breakers.

Q6
You want 100% tracing for a SPECIFIC user (x-user-id: test-user-42) to debug their session without tracing everyone. Task: How would you configure this? Explain the x-b3-flags: 1 force-sampling header and how it overrides the sampling rate. Write the curl command that forces a trace regardless of sampling percentage. Explain that this is a DEBUG feature — not for production use at scale.
Show Answer
Answer
# Force sampling for a specific request (debug only)
kubectl exec deploy/source -n anihpj -- \
  curl -s -H "x-b3-sampled: 1" \
          -H "x-b3-flags: 1" \
          -H "x-user-id: test-user-42" \
          http://jobpost-api/jobs/

# x-b3-sampled: 1 = this trace SHOULD be sampled
# x-b3-flags: 1   = FORCE sampling (overrides percentage)

How it works: When Envoy sees x-b3-flags: 1, it ignores the sampling percentage and ALWAYS traces this request. This allows targeted debugging without changing global config. Not for production use at scale — use it sparingly for specific debugging sessions.

Explanation

Force sampling via x-b3-flags: 1 is a powerful debug tool. It lets you trace specific requests without changing the global sampling config. On the ICA exam, this is useful when debugging a specific user's issue. The header propagates through the entire call chain — every downstream service also forces sampling for this trace. Best practice: combine with x-b3-sampled: 1 for clarity, but x-b3-flags: 1 alone is sufficient to force tracing.

Q7
Jaeger shows ZERO traces for the anihpj namespace, but Prometheus shows traffic is flowing. Task: Debug systematically: (a) verify sampling rate is not 0%, (b) verify Jaeger collector is running, (c) check if Envoy can reach Jaeger collector (port 14268), (d) verify istioctl proxy-config bootstrap shows the tracing configuration, (e) send a force-sampled request and check again. Write the fix for each possible failure.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Verify sampling > 0%
kubectl get telemetry -A
# Look for randomSamplingPercentage — must be > 0

# (b) Jaeger collector running?
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=jaeger
# ✅ Running
# ❌ Not found → install with: istioctl install --set profile=demo -y

# (c) Envoy → Jaeger collector connectivity (port 14268)
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- \
  curl -s http://jaeger-collector.istio-system:14268
# ✅ Reachable
# ❌ Connection refused → check Jaeger service and NetworkPolicy

# (d) Tracing config in Envoy bootstrap
istioctl proxy-config bootstrap deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep -A5 tracing
# ✅ Shows zipkin tracing provider with jaeger-collector address
# ❌ Empty → istiod hasn't pushed tracing config

# (e) Force a trace
kubectl exec deploy/source -n anihpj -- \
  curl -s -H "x-b3-flags: 1" http://jobpost-api/health
# Check Jaeger again — should show this trace
Explanation

Zero traces debugging follows this chain: sampling rate → Jaeger pod → Envoy connectivity → config in Envoy → force test. The most common cause: sampling rate is 0% (Telemetry not configured or meshConfig default is 0). Second most common: Jaeger collector not running (not installed with default profile). On the ICA exam, always check Telemetry resources FIRST before debugging infrastructure.

Q8
You want to correlate a specific trace with Prometheus metrics. Task: (a) In Jaeger, find a trace with status code 500 on user-service. (b) Note the timestamp. (c) In Prometheus, query for 5xx errors on user-service at that same timestamp. (d) Write the PromQL query that returns the error count in 1-minute windows. (e) Write a Grafana panel that overlays request rate and error rate on the same graph. Explain how Tracing (per-request detail) and Metrics (aggregate trends) complement each other.
Show Answer
Answer
# (d) PromQL: 5xx error count for user-service in 1-min windows
increase(istio_requests_total{
  destination_service="user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local",
  response_code=~"5.*"
}[1m])

# (e) Grafana panel: Overlay request rate + error rate
# Panel A (left Y-axis): Request rate
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
  destination_service="user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"}[5m]))

# Panel B (right Y-axis): Error rate %
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
  destination_service="user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local",
  response_code=~"5.*"}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
  destination_service="user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"}[5m]))
* 100

Metrics vs Tracing: Metrics = AGGREGATE (are errors happening? what's the rate?). Tracing = PER-REQUEST (WHY did THIS request fail? which service caused it?). Grafana shows you a spike in errors; Jaeger shows you the exact failing span.

Explanation

The observability workflow: Grafana alert fires ("user-service error rate > 5%") → Prometheus confirms the spike → Jaeger shows the slowest/failing trace → span details reveal root cause. Metrics tell you WHAT and WHEN; traces tell you WHY and WHERE. On the ICA exam, use this workflow: metrics for detection, traces for diagnosis. They're complementary — not interchangeable.

Q9
You need to verify that the Envoy sidecar is properly forwarding traces to Jaeger. Task: (a) Dump Envoy's bootstrap config and locate the tracing provider section. (b) Write the command to check the tracing cluster in Envoy's dynamic config. (c) Verify the Zipkin endpoint is correctly configured. (d) Send a force-sampled test request and confirm it appears in Jaeger. (e) Explain the Envoy → Jaeger communication path: Envoy sends spans to jaeger-collector.istio-system:9411 (Zipkin API).
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Bootstrap config — find tracing provider
istioctl proxy-config bootstrap deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep -A20 tracing
# ✅ Shows:
#   tracing:
#     http:
#       name: envoy.tracers.zipkin
#       typed_config:
#         collector_endpoint: /api/v2/spans
#         collector_cluster: jaeger-collector.istio-system

# (b) Check Jaeger cluster in dynamic config
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep jaeger
# ✅ outbound|9411||jaeger-collector.istio-system.svc.cluster.local

# (c) Verify Zipkin endpoint
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep jaeger
# ✅ Shows pod IP of jaeger-collector

# (d) Force-sampled test
kubectl exec deploy/source -n anihpj -- \
  curl -s -H "x-b3-flags: 1" http://jobpost-api/health
# Wait 10-30s, then check Jaeger UI

# (e) Communication path: Envoy → Zipkin API (port 9411) → Jaeger collector → Jaeger storage
Explanation

On the ICA exam, verify tracing end-to-end: bootstrap has the config → cluster exists → endpoint is reachable → spans appear in Jaeger. Envoy uses the Zipkin v2 API (/api/v2/spans) on port 9411 to send spans to Jaeger. If any link in this chain is broken, traces won't appear. The istioctl proxy-config bootstrap command shows the static (bootstrap) configuration; proxy-config cluster shows the dynamic cluster.

Q10
Comprehensive observability drill. Task: (a) Set tracing sampling to 100% in the anihpj namespace. (b) Generate 5 test requests with unique x-user-id headers. (c) Open Jaeger and find YOUR test traces. (d) For the slowest trace, identify the bottleneck span. (e) In Grafana, check if the service with the bottleneck span shows elevated p99 latency. (f) In Kiali, verify the service graph shows traffic on the edge to that service. (g) Fix: add a timeout to the slow service call via VirtualService. (h) Reset sampling to 1%. Write all commands in sequence.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Set 100% sampling
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: debug-tracing
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  tracing:
  - randomSamplingPercentage: 100.0
EOF

# (b) Generate 5 test requests with unique user IDs
for uid in test-user-{1..5}; do
  kubectl exec deploy/source -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s -H "x-user-id: $uid" http://jobpost-api/jobs/ &
done; wait

# (c) Open Jaeger
istioctl dashboard jaeger
# Search → Service: jobpost-api.anihpj → Sort: Longest Duration

# (d) Find slowest trace → identify bottleneck span (widest bar)

# (e) Check Grafana
istioctl dashboard grafana
# Istio Service Dashboard → select the bottleneck service → check p99 latency

# (f) Check Kiali
istioctl dashboard kiali
# Graph → anihpj namespace → verify edge to bottleneck service shows traffic

# (g) Fix: Add timeout
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: slow-service-timeout
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - skills-service   # example bottleneck
  http:
  - timeout: 2s
    route:
    - destination:
        host: skills-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
EOF

# (h) Reset sampling to 1%
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: debug-tracing
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  tracing:
  - randomSamplingPercentage: 1.0
EOF
Explanation

This is the complete observability workflow for the ICA exam. It integrates ALL four tools: Telemetry API (sampling config), Jaeger (trace analysis), Grafana (metrics dashboards), Kiali (topology), and VirtualService (the fix). The sequence: configure → generate → observe → diagnose → fix → restore defaults. Always reset sampling to production levels after debugging — 100% sampling adds CPU overhead.

Chapter 11: Kiali — Visualizing Your Entire Service Mesh

Kiali is the "control panel" for your Istio mesh. It shows a live service topology graph, validates your Istio configuration, and even generates YAML from a UI. Think of it as Google Maps for your microservices.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🗺️ Visualization 🎯 ICA 15%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Open and navigate the Kiali dashboard with istioctl dashboard kiali
  • ✅ Read the service graph: identify healthy (🟢), degraded (🟡), and failing (🔴) services
  • ✅ Click edges to see per-call-path metrics and jump directly to Jaeger traces
  • ✅ Validate Istio CRDs via Kiali's Istio Config tab
  • ✅ Use Kiali Wizards to generate VirtualService + DestinationRule YAML without coding
  • ✅ Verify mTLS by checking lock icons on graph edges
  • ✅ Monitor canary deployments: compare v1 vs v2 error rates and latency side-by-side
🎓 ICA Relevance
Observability 15%
💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 11
  • "Which service is unhealthy?" = Look for 🔴 RED nodes in Kiali graph
  • "Which call path is failing?" = Click the RED edge between two services
  • "Validate Istio configuration" = BOTH istioctl analyze AND Kiali Validation tab
  • "Generate canary YAML quickly" = Right-click service → Traffic Shifting wizard
  • "Verify mTLS" = Enable Security display → look for 🔒 green locks on all edges
  • CLI fallback: Kiali is visual — if it's down, use istioctl proxy-status + istioctl analyze
  • Kiali + Jaeger workflow: Red edge → click → View Traces → find slowest span

11.X Deep Dive — Kiali Diagnostic Workflow: From Alert to Root Cause

Kiali is not just a pretty graph — it's a diagnostic tool. Here's the recommended workflow when you get a production alert:

🔍 KIALI DIAGNOSTIC WORKFLOW — 6 Steps from Alert → Root Cause
  Step 1: Open Kiali → Filter namespace → OBSERVE COLORS
    🟢 Green nodes = healthy (200s, low latency) → SKIP
    🟡 Yellow nodes = degraded (some errors or high latency) → INVESTIGATE
    🔴 Red nodes = failing (high error rate, timeouts) → PRIORITY

  Step 2: HOVER over red node → Quick metrics popup
    RPS: 142 req/s  |  Error %: 37% (was 0.2% before)  →  SOMETHING CHANGED
    
  Step 3: FOLLOW RED EDGES upstream (who calls the failing service?)
    Click edge jobpost-api → payment-svc: Error % 82%  →  payment-svc is DOWN
    
  Step 4: DRILL INTO payment-svc node → View detailed metrics
    5xx Rate: 142/min  |  Latency p99: 12s (normally 200ms)  →  TIMEOUT pattern
    
  Step 5: Click Span → Open Jaeger traces for payment-svc
    Trace shows: payment-svc → Stripe API timing out at 10s  →  EXTERNAL DEPENDENCY
    
  Step 6: CHECK ISTIO CONFIG → "Istio Config" tab
    Are there validation errors on payment-svc's DestinationRule? →  FIX YAML
🧠 ICA Exam: Kiali Diagnostic Shortcuts

Kiali's Istio Config tab validates ALL of your YAML in one view — it catches: missing subsets, mismatched hosts, expired certs, invalid TLS config. On the ICA exam, if you're told "something is broken," open Kiali FIRST, check the Config tab for validation errors (red X marks), then follow the workflow above.

Q3
You notice a red edge from jobpost-api to user-service in Kiali. Task: (a) Click the red edge and note error percentage. (b) Click "View Traces" to jump to Jaeger. (c) Find the slowest/failing trace. (d) Check if OTHER callers to user-service also show red (isolate: caller or callee problem?). (e) Check mTLS lock icon — missing lock = mTLS mismatch causing 503.

Red edge → Jaeger is the fastest diagnostic path. If only jobpost-api→user-service is red, debug jobpost-api. If ALL callers show red, user-service is broken. Missing mTLS locks on edges often cause 503 errors.

Q4
Validate Istio CRDs in the anihpj namespace. Task: (a) Open Kiali → Istio Config → namespace: anihpj. (b) Find resources with red error icons. (c) Click an error to read validation message. (d) Run istioctl analyze -n anihpj and compare. (e) List 4 common config errors: missing subsets, port name issues, host mismatches, mTLS conflicts.
Show Answer
Answer

Kiali Validation and istioctl analyze are equivalent — both catch ~80% of config errors. Kiali is visual (click for details), CLI is scriptable. Use both: Kiali for discovery, CLI for exact error messages.

Explanation

🔒 Part 7: Security — Zero Trust with Istio Chapters 12-13

Chapter 12: Mutual TLS (mTLS) — Encrypting Everything

Inside a Kubernetes cluster, traffic is plain HTTP by default. Any compromised pod can sniff passwords, tokens, and PII from other services. Istio's mTLS encrypts ALL service-to-service traffic automatically — without changing a single line of code.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔒 Security 🎯 ICA 25%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand mTLS: BOTH sides prove identity (unlike regular TLS — server only)
  • ✅ Apply PeerAuthentication with PERMISSIVE (migration) and STRICT (enforce) modes
  • ✅ Verify mTLS via Kiali lock icons, istioctl proxy-config secret, istioctl authn tls-check
  • ✅ Know SPIFFE identity format: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api
  • ✅ Debug mTLS 503s: align DestinationRule TLS mode (client) with PeerAuthentication (server)
  • ✅ Certificates auto-rotate every 24h, managed by istiod — zero downtime, zero manual renewal
🎓 ICA Relevance
Security 25%
💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapters 12-13 (Security — 25%)
  • "Encrypt all service traffic" = PeerAuthentication mode: STRICT
  • "Restrict which service can call which" = AuthorizationPolicy
  • "Validate JWT tokens at mesh level" = RequestAuthentication
  • Remember: mTLS = identity (WHO), AuthzPolicy = permissions (WHAT)

12.1 The Security Problem Without mTLS

Without Istio, your Kubernetes cluster has three critical attack vectors open right now:

🔴 WITHOUT ISTIO — 3 Attack Vectors Open
👃
ATTACK 1: Sniffing

Rogue pod on same node runs tcpdump → captures all plain HTTP between services. JWT tokens, passwords, PII — all visible in plaintext.

🎭
ATTACK 2: Impersonation

Attacker deploys a pod named "user-service" → jobpost-api connects to the fake service → returns fake data, steals real requests.

🦶
ATTACK 3: Lateral Movement

Compromised skills-service calls user-service → exfiltrates ALL user data. Any service can call any other service.

🟢 WITH ISTIO — All 3 Attacks Blocked
🔒
DEFENSE 1: mTLS

All traffic encrypted. Rogue pod sees only binary garbage. SPIFFE certificates auto-issued by istiod.

🪪
DEFENSE 2: SPIFFE Identity

Fake service has no valid certificate. Envoy rejects: "Not spiffe://.../ns/anihpj/sa/user-service".

🚫
DEFENSE 3: AuthzPolicy

AuthorizationPolicy: ALLOW from jobpost-api ONLY → skills-service request → 403 Forbidden.

12.2 What is Mutual TLS (mTLS)?

Regular TLS: server proves identity to client (like HTTPS websites). Mutual TLS: BOTH sides prove identity to each other. Istio issues X.509 SVID certificates (SPIFFE standard) to every workload automatically.

🤝 mTLS HANDSHAKE — What Happens in Every Service Call
1
Envoy(jobpost)

"Hello, I am jobpost-api"
Presents SPIFFE cert (SVID)

2
Envoy(user)

"I am user-service"
Presents SPIFFE cert (SVID)

3
Verify

Both verify with istiod
Cert: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api

4
Encrypt

mTLS tunnel established 🔒
GET /users/42 sent encrypted

✅
Done!

Zero code change in Django!
Certs auto-rotate every 24h

📖 SPIFFE Identity Format

Each certificate contains: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api-serviceaccount. This identifies the service, not the node or IP. Even if an attacker gets the same IP, they can't get the same SPIFFE identity without the certificate.

12.3 PeerAuthentication — Configuring mTLS Mode

PeerAuthentication is the Istio CRD that controls mTLS. Three modes: PERMISSIVE (migration), STRICT (enforce), DISABLE (debug only).

yaml — PeerAuthentication for anihpj 

# Enforce STRICT mTLS for entire anihpj namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT       # ALL traffic must use mTLS
                       # Plain HTTP will be REJECTED

# Per-workload: only user-service requires STRICT
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: user-service-mtls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: user-service
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
🔄 MIGRATION PATH — PERMISSIVE → STRICT
Week 1
PERMISSIVE
Accept both HTTP + mTLS
No disruption
Week 2
STRICT per namespace
Non-sidecar → 403 errors
Fix: inject sidecars
RESULT
All traffic encrypted ✅
Kiali shows lock icons
Zero Django code changes

12.4 Certificate Lifecycle — How istiod Issues Certs

Every pod gets an X.509 certificate at startup from istiod's built-in CA. Certs auto-rotate every 24 hours — no manual renewal needed.

🔄 CERTIFICATE LIFECYCLE — Full Flow for anihpj
T=0
Pod Deployed

kubectl apply → Pod created

0.1s
Sidecar Injected

Webhook adds istio-proxy

0.3s
CSR Sent

Proxy → istiod:15012
spiffe://.../sa/jobpost-api

0.5s
Cert Issued

istiod validates SA → signs X.509 cert (24h expiry)

0.7s
mTLS Ready

Cert in-memory. All calls now use mTLS!

23h55m
Auto-Rotate

5min before expiry → new CSR → new cert → seamless!

💡 Cert Anatomy

Subject: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api-serviceaccount

Issuer: istiod (cluster.local root CA) · Valid: 24 hours · SANs: SPIFFE URI

Rotation: Every 24h, rotated 5min before expiry. Zero downtime. You never need to manually renew certificates.

12.5 Secure Naming — Preventing Service Impersonation

Secure naming is a critical Istio security concept from the official docs. It answers: "Is this SPIFFE identity allowed to run this service?" Without it, an attacker with a valid certificate for one service could impersonate another.

🎭 IMPERSONATION ATTACK — How Secure Naming Defeats It
ATTACK SCENARIO:
  Attacker compromises test-team's service account → gets valid SPIFFE cert
  Attacker deploys fake user-service pod with test-team's cert
  DNS spoofing redirects jobpost-api traffic to fake user-service

WITHOUT Secure Naming:  ❌ Attack succeeds
  jobpost-api Envoy sees valid SPIFFE cert → trusts it → sends data

WITH Secure Naming:     ✅ Attack BLOCKED
  jobpost-api Envoy checks: "Is spiffe://.../sa/test-team authorized
  to run user-service?"
  → istiod's secure naming map says: NO. Only spiffe://.../sa/user-service
    is authorized to run user-service.
  → Connection REJECTED — authentication fails!

🔑 Secure Naming Map (maintained by istiod):
  spiffe://.../sa/jobpost-api  → jobpost-api  ✅
  spiffe://.../sa/user-service → user-service ✅
  spiffe://.../sa/test-team    → test-service ✅
  spiffe://.../sa/test-team    → user-service ❌ NOT AUTHORIZED
💡 ICA Exam Relevance

While secure naming is automatic in Istio (istiod maintains the mapping, Envoy enforces it), understanding it helps answer questions about "why can't an attacker impersonate a service even with a valid certificate?" The answer: Secure naming — the SPIFFE identity must match the service name in istiod's registry.

12.6 PeerAuthentication Policy Hierarchy — Mesh → Namespace → Workload

From the official docs: PeerAuthentication policies follow a strict narrowest-match-wins hierarchy. Understanding this prevents configuration surprises:

ScopeSelectorApplies ToPriority
Mesh-wideNo selector, root namespaceALL workloads in meshLowest (fallback)
Namespace-wideNo selector, specific namespaceAll workloads in that namespaceMedium
Workload-specificselector.matchLabels: setOnly matching podsHighest (overrides all)
⚠️ Key Rules from Official Docs

Only ONE mesh-wide and ONE namespace-wide PeerAuthentication can exist. If you create multiple, newer ones are IGNORED. Workload-specific policies can coexist — the oldest one wins when multiple match. This is different from RequestAuthentication, where ALL matching policies are combined.

12.X mTLS Troubleshooting — Common Scenarios and Solutions

🔴 Symptom🔍 Most Likely Cause✅ Fix
503 after enabling STRICTNon-Istio pods in namespaceInject sidecars or use PERMISSIVE temporarily
New pod can't start after STRICTistiod unreachable for CSRCheck istiod pod health, port 15012 reachable
mTLS works but AuthorizationPolicy blocksNo ALLOW policy created after deny-allCreate specific ALLOW AuthorizationPolicy
Cross-namespace call failsPA STRICT in target ns, PERMISSIVE in sourceApply consistent PeerAuthentication across namespaces
Certificate expiredistiod CA not issuing/renewingCheck istiod logs, restart pod to force new CSR
🔄 SPIFFE CERTIFICATE LIFECYCLE — From Issuance to Rotation
🔑
STEP 1
CSR Generated

Auto

STEP 2
istiod Validates

istiod checks ServiceAccount existence, namespace, pod identity

12.Z Deep Dive — RequestAuthentication: End-User JWT Authentication

While PeerAuthentication verifies service-to-service identity (SPIFFE mTLS), RequestAuthentication verifies end-user identity using JSON Web Tokens (JWT). This is how you authenticate human users or external API clients at the mesh level — no application code changes needed.

🪪 REQUEST AUTHENTICATION FLOW — JWT Validation at the Gateway
  1. User sends request with: Authorization: Bearer <JWT_TOKEN>
  2. Ingress Gateway Envoy intercepts request
  3. RequestAuthentication policy tells Envoy: "Validate JWT for issuer X using JWKS at URL Y"
  4. Envoy fetches public keys from JWKS endpoint → validates signature
  5. If valid: forward to backend with request.auth.principal populated
  6. If invalid/missing: by default, STILL forwards (401 only if AuthorizationPolicy enforces it)
  
  ⚠️ CRITICAL: RequestAuthentication alone does NOT reject requests!
  It only VALIDATES. To REJECT, you need an AuthorizationPolicy with DENY action.
PeerAuthentication
  • Service-to-service identity
  • Uses SPIFFE X.509 certificates
  • Modes: STRICT / PERMISSIVE / DISABLE
  • source.principal populated
  • No JWT involved
RequestAuthentication
  • End-user / API client identity
  • Uses JWT tokens (OIDC/OAuth2)
  • Validates: issuer, audience, expiry, signature
  • request.auth.principal populated
  • Requires JWKS endpoint (public key set)
📝 RequestAuthentication YAML Example
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jwt-auth
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      istio: ingressgateway  # Apply to ingress gateway
  jwtRules:
  - issuer: "https://auth.anihpj.com"
    jwksUri: "https://auth.anihpj.com/.well-known/jwks.json"
    audiences: ["jobpost-api"]
    fromHeaders:
    - name: Authorization
      prefix: "Bearer "
    forwardOriginalToken: true  # Pass JWT to backend
🔗 JWT + AuthorizationPolicy — Requiring Valid Tokens
# Step 1: RequestAuthentication VALIDATES the JWT
# (Above policy)

# Step 2: AuthorizationPolicy REJECTS requests without valid JWT
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-jwt
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      istio: ingressgateway
  action: DENY
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        notRequestPrincipals: ["*"]  # No valid JWT → DENY
JWT StatusRequestAuthentication+ AuthZ Policy (above)
No token✅ 200 (passes through)❌ 403 (DENY: no principal)
Valid token✅ 200 (principal set)✅ 200 (has principal)
Invalid/expired token❌ 401 (validation fails)❌ 401 (same)
⚠️ ICA Exam: The 60-Second JWT Clock Skew

Istio allows 60 seconds of clock skew for JWT validation. A token becomes valid 60 seconds BEFORE its nbf (not before) time and remains valid 60 seconds AFTER its exp (expiry) time. If a question shows a token expiring at T+5s and still working at T+65s — that's the 60s skew, not a bug.

12.X Deep Dive — The DR/PA TLS Contract (Why 503s Happen)

The most common mTLS 503 debugging scenario: DR and PA TLS modes don't match.

🤝 TLS CONTRACT MATRIX
  DR (Client)          PA (Server)        Result
  ISTIO_MUTUAL   +     STRICT       =     ✅ mTLS works
  ISTIO_MUTUAL   +     PERMISSIVE   =     ✅ Works (mTLS accepted)
  DISABLE        +     STRICT       =     ❌ 503 — client sends plain, server requires mTLS
  DISABLE        +     PERMISSIVE   =     ✅ Works (plain accepted)
  ISTIO_MUTUAL   +     DISABLE      =     ⚠️ Client sends mTLS, server expects none — may fail
  
  Debug: istioctl authn tls-check deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj

12.X SPIRE Integration — External Certificate Authority for Istio

By default, Istio uses its built-in CA (istiod) to issue SPIFFE X.509 SVID certificates. But for enterprise environments requiring FIPS 140-2 compliance, hardware security modules (HSM), or centralized PKI, you can replace istiod's CA with SPIRE — the CNCF SPIFFE Runtime Environment.

🔐 DEFAULT CA (istiod) vs EXTERNAL CA (SPIRE) — Architecture
Default: istiod CA
  • istiod generates a self-signed root CA at install
  • Stores root cert in cacerts Kubernetes secret
  • Auto-rotates workload certs every 24 hours
  • Simple, zero-config, no external dependencies
  • ✅ Best for most deployments
External: SPIRE
  • SPIRE Server + SPIRE Agents on each node
  • Plugs into enterprise PKI, Vault, HSM backends
  • FIPS 140-2 compliant cryptography
  • Multi-cluster, multi-cloud identity federation
  • ✅ Best for regulated industries (finance, government)
🔄 SPIRE CERTIFICATE FLOW — How Workloads Get Identity
  1. SPIRE Agent on Node → registers workload with SPIRE Server
  2. SPIRE Server → validates workload identity (K8s SA, labels)
  3. SPIRE Server → issues SPIFFE SVID → pushes to Agent
  4. SPIRE Agent → writes SVID to Unix Domain Socket (UDS)
  5. Envoy → reads SVID from UDS via SDS (Secret Discovery Service)
  6. Envoy → presents SVID to peers for mTLS handshake
  
  SVID format: spiffe://example.org/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api
  (trust domain = example.org, not cluster.local)
💡 ICA Exam: When to Use SPIRE

The ICA exam may ask about external CA scenarios. Key signals: "FIPS compliance required," "use existing PKI," "HSM integration," "multi-trust-domain federation." Default answer for most scenarios: istiod's built-in CA is sufficient. SPIRE is for specific enterprise requirements.

12.W Deep Dive — Plug-in Your Own CA Certificates: Enterprise PKI Integration

Instead of using istiod's self-signed root CA, you can plug in your own enterprise root CA, intermediate CA certs, and signing key. This is a separate concept from SPIRE — here you're still using istiod as the CA, but with your own certificate chain.

🏛️ CA HIERARCHY — Multi-Cluster with One Root CA
  ROOT CA (Offline, HSM-protected)
  │  Signs intermediate CAs for each cluster
  ├── Intermediate CA: cluster1  → istiod signs workload certs for cluster1
  ├── Intermediate CA: cluster2  → istiod signs workload certs for cluster2
  └── Intermediate CA: cluster3  → istiod signs workload certs for cluster3
  
  RESULT: All clusters share the same root of trust → cross-cluster mTLS works
  
  SECRET STRUCTURE (cacerts secret in istio-system):
  ca-cert.pem     = Intermediate CA certificate (istiod signs with this)
  ca-key.pem      = Intermediate CA private key
  root-cert.pem   = Root CA certificate (distributed to all workloads)
  cert-chain.pem  = Full chain: intermediate → root
# Step 1: Generate root CA
make -f tools/certs/Makefile.selfsigned.mk root-ca
# Output: root-cert.pem, root-key.pem

# Step 2: Generate intermediate CA for each cluster
make -f tools/certs/Makefile.selfsigned.mk cluster1-cacerts
# Output: cluster1/{ca-cert.pem, ca-key.pem, cert-chain.pem, root-cert.pem}

# Step 3: Create cacerts secret (MUST be named "cacerts")
kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system \
  --from-file=cluster1/ca-cert.pem \
  --from-file=cluster1/ca-key.pem \
  --from-file=cluster1/root-cert.pem \
  --from-file=cluster1/cert-chain.pem

# Step 4: Install Istio — it detects cacerts secret automatically
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y
💡 ICA: cacerts Secret Name is MAGIC

The secret MUST be named cacerts in the istio-system namespace. Istio automatically detects it at startup. If present, istiod uses these certs instead of generating a self-signed root. For multi-cluster: share the SAME root-cert.pem across all clusters — this is what enables cross-cluster mTLS with a unified trust domain.

📝 Chapter 12 — ICA Practice Questions (Hands-On Lab Scenarios)

Q1
Your ICA exam terminal has Istio installed with PERMISSIVE mTLS. Task: (a) Write a PeerAuthentication that enforces STRICT mTLS for the anihpj namespace. (b) Verify mTLS is active using Kiali (lock icons) and istioctl proxy-config secret. (c) Test by curling between services — verify 200 OK. (d) Explain the SPIFFE identity format: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api. (e) What happens if a pod WITHOUT a sidecar tries to call a service in a STRICT namespace?
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: anihpj-strict-mtls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

Verify: Kiali edges show 🔒 lock icons. istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj shows SPIFFE cert. Sidecar-less pod → 403 Forbidden — no SPIFFE cert to present.

Explanation

PeerAuthentication STRICT is the ICA exam answer to "encrypt all service traffic." Every incoming connection MUST present a SPIFFE cert. Non-mesh pods are immediately rejected with 403.

Q2
You need to migrate anihpj to mTLS without breaking existing traffic. Task: (a) Start with PERMISSIVE mode. (b) Verify all services have sidecars (2/2). (c) Verify Kiali shows mixed lock icons. (d) Once confirmed, switch to STRICT. (e) Write the complete 4-step migration checklist with commands. Explain why PERMISSIVE first is critical.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Apply PERMISSIVE
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata: {name: default, namespace: anihpj}
spec: {mtls: {mode: PERMISSIVE}}
EOF
# 2. Verify all pods 2/2
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# 3. Check Kiali — locks appear on edges
istioctl dashboard kiali
# 4. Switch to STRICT
kubectl patch peerauthentication default -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/mtls/mode","value":"STRICT"}]'

PERMISSIVE first = safe coexistence. STRICT immediately blocks all plaintext — if any service lacks a sidecar, it breaks.

Explanation

Migration path: PERMISSIVE → verify → STRICT. This is the ICA exam's recommended mTLS rollout. Never go straight to STRICT.

Q3
Verify mTLS is working end-to-end. Task: (a) Run istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj and identify the SPIFFE cert, expiration date, and trust chain. (b) Run istioctl authn tls-check deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj. (c) Open Kiali with Security display and verify ALL edges have green locks. (d) Explain: certs auto-rotate every 24h, 5 minutes before expiry, managed by istiod — zero downtime.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
# Shows: default certificate, ROOTCA, credentialName
# Expiration: ~24h from now

istioctl authn tls-check deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
# Shows per-port mTLS status, cert validity

Cert rotation: auto, every 24h, istiod handles it transparently. Envoy gets new cert before old expires. Zero connection drops.

Explanation

Three verification methods. Cert rotation is fully automatic — you never touch certs. Know this for the ICA exam.

Q4
Apply STRICT mTLS to only ONE specific workload. Task: Write a PeerAuthentication that applies STRICT only to user-service (label app: user-service), leaving other services in PERMISSIVE. Verify: curl user-service from a sidecar → 200 OK. curl user-service from a non-sidecar pod → 403. Explain the precedence: workload-specific overrides namespace-wide.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: user-service-strict
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: user-service
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

Workload-specific policies OVERRIDE namespace-wide. If namespace is PERMISSIVE but workload is STRICT → STRICT wins for that workload.

Explanation

Selective enforcement: apply STRICT to sensitive services first, gradually expand. Precedence: workload > namespace > mesh.

Q5
You applied STRICT mTLS and now jobpost-api can't call user-service — 503 errors. Task: Debug: (a) Check DestinationRule TLS mode for user-service. (b) Verify it's ISTIO_MUTUAL (client side). (c) Verify PeerAuthentication is STRICT (server side). (d) Run istioctl authn tls-check on both services. (e) Fix: align DR TLS mode with PA. Explain the DR/PA contract.
Show Answer
Answer
# Client side — MUST be ISTIO_MUTUAL
kubectl get destinationrule -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 tls:
# tls: mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL  ✅
# tls: mode: DISABLE        ❌ Client sends plaintext, server requires mTLS = 503

# Fix:
kubectl patch destinationrule user-service-dr -n anihpj --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/trafficPolicy/tls/mode","value":"ISTIO_MUTUAL"}]'

DR = client (what to send). PA = server (what to accept). Both must agree. ISTIO_MUTUAL + STRICT = working mTLS.

Explanation

The TLS contract: DR decides what outbound Envoy sends, PA decides what inbound Envoy accepts. Mismatch = 503. Always check both.

Q6
Use Kiali to verify mTLS for the entire mesh. Task: (a) Enable Security display in Kiali Graph. (b) Verify every edge has a 🔒 green lock. (c) Find any edge WITHOUT a lock — that service pair has broken mTLS. (d) Click the edge to see mTLS status. (e) Explain the 3 phases: No locks (DISABLE) → Mixed locks (PERMISSIVE) → All green (STRICT).
Show Answer
Answer

Kiali Security display shows: 🔒 green = ISTIO_MUTUAL working, no lock = DISABLE, gray lock = PERMISSIVE. Migrate left to right: DISABLE → PERMISSIVE → STRICT.

Explanation

Kiali is the fastest mTLS verification on the ICA exam. All green locks = full mTLS deployment complete.

Q7
Verify mTLS end-to-end using three methods. Task: (a) Kiali: enable Security display → verify 🔒 green locks on ALL edges between anihpj services. (b) CLI: istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj → find SPIFFE cert, note expiration (~24h). (c) CLI: istioctl authn tls-check deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj → verify per-port mTLS status. (d) Explain which method is fastest (Kiali) vs most detailed (tls-check).
Show Answer
Answer

Kiali = fastest (visual lock icons). tls-check = most detailed (per-port, cert chain, expiration). proxy-config secret = raw cert inspection. Use all three: Kiali for overview → tls-check for detail → secret for raw cert.

Explanation

Three verification methods from fastest to most detailed. Kiali lock icons are the quickest verification on the ICA exam.

Q8
A non-Istio pod gets 403 after STRICT mTLS is applied. Task: (a) Verify the pod shows 1/1 (no sidecar). (b) Check PeerAuthentication mode. (c) Fix options: (1) inject sidecar by labeling its namespace, (2) temporarily use PERMISSIVE, (3) apply STRICT only to specific workloads via selector. (d) Explain: STRICT means ALL callers need SPIFFE certs — non-mesh pods can't comply. Always verify all communicating services have sidecars before STRICT.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj

STRICT = zero trust. Every connection must present a valid SPIFFE cert. Non-mesh pods → 403.

Explanation

Most common mTLS migration issue. Always inject sidecars BEFORE switching to STRICT, or use PERMISSIVE temporarily.

Q9
Explain the certificate chain and auto-rotation. Task: (a) Run istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj and identify: root CA, workload cert, expiration time. (b) Explain the chain: Root CA (istiod) → Intermediate CA → Workload SVID. (c) Cert rotation: every 24h, auto-rotated 5 min before expiry, zero downtime. (d) What if istiod is DOWN during rotation? Envoy uses cached cert until istiod recovers. (e) Compare with external CA: istiod forwards CSRs to Vault/Cert-Manager.
Show Answer
Answer

Chain: Root CA (auto-created) → Intermediate CA (optional) → SVID (per workload, 24h TTL). Rotation: auto, transparent, no downtime. External CA: istiod becomes RA, forwarding CSRs.

Explanation

Certificate management is fully automatic. Root CA is auto-created. Rotation is transparent. External CA for enterprise PKI.

Q10
Integrate an external CA like Vault or Cert-Manager. Task: (a) Configure meshConfig.ca.externalCa with the external CA's address and TLS settings. (b) istiod acts as a Registration Authority — it forwards CSR requests from Envoy to the external CA for signing. (c) Alternative: mount external CA cert and key directly. (d) Explain use case: enterprises with existing PKI infrastructure that must be used for compliance. (e) Compare: built-in CA (simpler, auto) vs external CA (compliance, existing PKI).
Show Answer
Answer

External CA: meshConfig.ca.externalCa → istiod forwards CSRs. Enterprise PKI integration for compliance. Mounted cert alternative also available.

Explanation

External CA for enterprise PKI compliance. istiod becomes an RA, not a CA. Advanced security topic on the ICA exam.

Chapter 13: Authorization Policies — Who Can Call What

mTLS proves identity, but doesn't restrict access. Without AuthorizationPolicy, any service with a valid cert can call any other service. AuthorizationPolicy is Istio's Layer 7 firewall — you define exactly WHO can call WHAT, using WHICH methods, on WHICH paths.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🛡️ Access Control 🎯 ICA 25%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Build zero-trust: deny-all first (empty spec), then create selective ALLOW policies
  • ✅ Understand evaluation order: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW (DENY always beats ALLOW)
  • ✅ Restrict by SPIFFE principal (service identity), HTTP method, path, headers, and JWT claims
  • ✅ Differentiate mTLS (WHO = identity) from AuthorizationPolicy (WHAT = permissions)
  • ✅ Use RequestAuthentication for JWT validation + AuthorizationPolicy for JWT-based access control
  • ✅ Combine SPIFFE + JWT for defense-in-depth: both service AND user must be authorized
🎓 ICA Relevance
Security 25%
💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 13
  • "Deny all traffic" = AuthorizationPolicy with empty spec: {} — no rules = nothing allowed
  • "Allow specific caller" = ALLOW rule with principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
  • "First policy applied" = Default switches from ALLOW-ALL to DENY-ALL — only explicit ALLOWs pass
  • DENY > ALLOW: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW. If DENY matches → immediate 403 regardless of ALLOW
  • JWT auth: RequestAuthentication validates tokens, AuthorizationPolicy enforces based on claims
  • 3 security layers: mTLS (encryption+service ID) → AuthzPolicy (service permissions) → JWT (user identity)

13.1 The Need for Service-Level Authorization

mTLS ensures the caller IS who they claim to be. But should a compromised skills-service be allowed to call user-service and read all user data? With zero-trust, the answer is NO. Every call must be explicitly authorized.

⚠️ CRITICAL — mTLS ≠ Authorization

Even with STRICT mTLS, without AuthorizationPolicy, ANY service can call ANY other service. mTLS proves identity but doesn't restrict permissions. You need BOTH: mTLS for encryption + identity, AuthorizationPolicy for access control.

13.2 AuthorizationPolicy — The Istio Firewall

AuthorizationPolicy works at Layer 7 (HTTP). You can allow/deny based on: source identity (SPIFFE), HTTP method (GET/POST/DELETE), HTTP path, headers, and source namespace.

🔍 AUTHORIZATION POLICY EVALUATION — How Istio Decides
1
Request

skills-service → GET /users/42 → user-service

2
CUSTOM?

Custom policy exists? Evaluate first

3
DENY?

Matching DENY policy? → DENY ❌

4
ALLOW?

Matching ALLOW policy? → ALLOW ✅

5
Default

No matching ALLOW → DENY ❌

Result
403

skills-service NOT in allow-list for user-service

yaml — Complete AuthorizationPolicy for anihpj 

# Step 1: Deny ALL traffic in anihpj namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: anihpj
spec: {}                        # ← empty spec = deny everything
---
# Step 2: Allow ingress → jobpost-api (GET/POST only)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-to-jobpost
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:
        - "cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/istio-ingressgateway"
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
---
# Step 3: Allow jobpost-api → user-service (GET only)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-jobpost-to-users
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: user-service
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:
        - "cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET"]
        paths: ["/api/users/*"]

13.3 Building a Zero-Trust Policy for anihpj

Step-by-step: deny everything → allow specific paths only. Here's the complete policy matrix:

🔐 ZERO-TRUST POLICY MATRIX — anihpj

SourceTargetAllowed Methods
istio-ingressgatewayjobpost-apiGET, POST
jobpost-apiuser-serviceGET only
jobpost-apiskills-serviceGET only
jobpost-apilocation-serviceGET only
user-serviceauth-serviceGET, POST
PrometheusALL servicesGET /metrics
ANY OTHERANY❌ DENIED
💡 ICA Exam Tip

If ANY AuthorizationPolicy targets a workload, all requests NOT explicitly ALLOWed are DENIED. The default "allow all" only applies when ZERO policies target that workload.

13.4 RequestAuthentication — JWT Verification at the Mesh Level

Validate JWT tokens at the Istio layer — no auth code needed in every Django service. Istio verifies the JWT signature and extracts claims for use in AuthorizationPolicy conditions.

yaml — RequestAuthentication + JWT-based AuthorizationPolicy 

# Verify JWT tokens from auth-service
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jwt-auth
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  jwtRules:
  - issuer: "auth-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
    jwksUri: "http://auth-service/.well-known/jwks.json"
---
# Allow only requests with valid JWT containing role=admin
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-admin-jwt
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - when:
    - key: request.auth.claims[role]
      values: ["admin"]

13.5 Exclusion Matching — "NOT" Conditions in AuthorizationPolicy

From the official docs: AuthorizationPolicy supports exclusion matching using notPaths, notValues, notIpBlocks, and notPrincipals. This allows you to say "apply this policy to everything EXCEPT..." — a powerful pattern for health checks and public endpoints:

🩺
Pattern 1: Skip JWT for Health Checks
rules:
- to:
  - operation:
      notPaths: ["/healthz", "/ready"]
  from:
  - source:
      requestPrincipals: ["*"]

Requires JWT for ALL paths EXCEPT /healthz and /ready. Health probes bypass auth.

🚫
Pattern 2: Deny External to Admin
action: DENY
rules:
- to:
  - operation:
      paths: ["/admin"]
  from:
  - source:
      notNamespaces: ["anihpj"]

Denies /admin access from ANY namespace EXCEPT anihpj.

📋 EXCLUSION MATCHING FIELDS — What You Can Negate

Exclusion FieldUsageExample
notPathsAll paths EXCEPT thesenotPaths: ["/public"]
notValuesAll values EXCEPT these (when conditions)notValues: ["hack"]
notIpBlocksAll IPs EXCEPT thesenotIpBlocks: ["10.0.0.0/8"]
notNamespacesAll namespaces EXCEPT thesenotNamespaces: ["external"]
notPrincipalsAll identities EXCEPT thesenotPrincipals: ["cluster.local/..."]
notRequestPrincipalsAll JWT principals EXCEPT thesenotRequestPrincipals: ["*"]

13.6 TCP Authorization — Protecting Non-HTTP Workloads

From the official docs: AuthorizationPolicy works for any plain TCP protocol (MongoDB, Redis, MySQL, Kafka), not just HTTP. The difference: HTTP-only fields (hosts, methods, paths, requestPrincipals) are ignored for TCP traffic. Only ports, principals, namespaces, and ipBlocks apply.

yaml — TCP AuthZ: Only jobpost-api can access MongoDB on port 27017 
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: mongodb-policy
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: mongodb
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
    to:
    - operation:
        ports: ["27017"]          # ← ONLY port-level control for TCP
⚠️ Important: mTLS Dependency for Principal-Based Rules

From the official docs: if you use principals, namespaces, or source.principal in AuthorizationPolicy, mTLS MUST be enabled. These fields derive from SPIFFE certificates — without mTLS, they're empty or spoofable. Always pair principal-based AuthZ with PeerAuthentication STRICT.

13.X Deep Dive — AuthorizationPolicy Evaluation with Real Requests

Understanding the EXACT evaluation order is critical for the ICA exam. Let's walk through 3 real requests and see how Istio decides ALLOW or DENY.

🔍 EVALUATION ORDER — CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW (DENY always beats ALLOW)
REQUEST 1: jobpost-api → GET /api/users/42 → user-service
  Step 1: CUSTOM policies? → None
  Step 2: DENY policies? → "deny-skills" checks: source=skills-service? → NO match
  Step 3: ALLOW policies? → "allow-jobpost" checks: source=jobpost-api? → YES ✅
  Step 4: All conditions met? → YES → ALLOW ✅ (200 OK)

REQUEST 2: skills-service → GET /api/users/42 → user-service
  Step 1: CUSTOM policies? → None
  Step 2: DENY policies? → "deny-skills" checks: source=skills-service? → YES ❌
  RESULT: DENY (403 Forbidden) — evaluation STOPS here, ALLOW never checked

REQUEST 3: No AuthZ policies at all → user-service
  Step 1: CUSTOM? → None. Step 2: DENY? → None. Step 3: ALLOW? → None.
  RESULT: Default ALLOW (200 OK) — no policy = everything allowed
⚠️ CRITICAL: First Policy Changes Default

The moment you create ANY AuthorizationPolicy targeting a workload, the default switches from ALLOW-ALL to DENY-ALL. Only explicitly ALLOWed requests pass. Always create a deny-all (spec: {}) FIRST, then add selective ALLOW policies.

🛡️ Authorization — Visual Recap

🚫
Deny All
Empty spec = deny
✅
ALLOW
Explicit allow-list
🪪
Principals
SPIFFE identity
🔑
JWT
Mesh-level auth
L7
L7 Firewall

🛡️

13.Y Deep Dive — AuthorizationPolicy Advanced: Exclusion Matching, Custom Conditions & ClusterTrustBundle

Beyond basic ALLOW/DENY rules, the official Istio docs describe several advanced AuthorizationPolicy features critical for real-world security:

🚫 Exclusion Matching — "NOT" Conditions

Use notPaths, notIpBlocks, notPorts, and notRequestPrincipals to exclude specific conditions:

# Allow access to ALL paths EXCEPT /admin (no JWT required for /healthz)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-except-admin
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - to:
    - operation:
        notPaths: ["/admin"]  # ALL paths allowed EXCEPT /admin
    from:
    - source:
        requestPrincipals: ["*"]  # Requires valid JWT
---
# Allow unauthenticated access ONLY to /healthz
  - to:
    - operation:
        paths: ["/healthz"]  # Health check: no auth needed
# (no 'from' clause = anyone can access)
🔧 Custom Conditions — The "when" Clause

Match on ANY Istio attribute using the when field. Supported keys include request.headers, request.auth.claims, source.ip, destination.port, and more:

spec:
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET"]
    when:
    - key: request.headers[x-api-version]
      values: ["v2", "v3"]  # Only requests with specific header value
    - key: request.auth.claims[iss]
      values: ["https://auth.anihpj.com"]  # Must come from specific issuer
📦 ClusterTrustBundle — Trust Distribution (Istio 1.28+)

ClusterTrustBundle is a Kubernetes CRD (certificates.k8s.io/v1alpha1) that Istio now supports for distributing trusted CA bundles cluster-wide. Instead of manually mounting CA certs, you create a ClusterTrustBundle and Istio uses it for certificate validation:

apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterTrustBundle
metadata:
  name: anihpj-custom-ca
spec:
  trustBundle: |
    -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
    MIIDXTCCAkWgAwIBAgIJAKl...
    -----END CERTIFICATE-----

Enable in Istio: --set values.pilot.env.ENABLE_CLUSTER_TRUST_BUNDLE_API=true. Requires K8s 1.27+.

🧠 ICA Exam: Evaluation Order is CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW

For each request, Istio checks: (1) CUSTOM policies — delegates to external auth system. (2) DENY policies — if ANY deny policy matches → 403 immediately. (3) ALLOW policies — if ANY allow policy matches → 200. If no ALLOW policy matches → 403 (deny-by-default when at least one ALLOW policy exists). Key insight: Without any ALLOW policy at all, ALL traffic is allowed. Adding the FIRST ALLOW policy activates deny-by-default.

13.Z Deep Dive — Dry Run Authorization: Test Policies Without Breaking Traffic

From the official docs: Dry-run authorization lets you test an AuthorizationPolicy before enforcing it. Add the annotation istio.io/dry-run: "true" and Istio will shadow-evaluate the policy — logging what WOULD be denied while still allowing all traffic through.

🧪 DRY RUN AUTHZ — Test Before You Enforce
  WITHOUT Dry Run (risky):
  Apply DENY policy → 5 minutes later → "Why is production broken?!" → PANIC ROLLBACK
  
  WITH Dry Run (safe):
  Apply DENY policy with dry-run annotation → Traffic still flows normally →
  Check 3 output channels → Adjust policy → Remove annotation → Enforce safely
  
  OUTPUT CHANNELS:
  1. Proxy Logs:  "shadow denied, matched policy ns[foo]-policy[name]-rule[0]"
  2. Prometheus:  envoy_http_inbound_*_rbac{authz_dry_run_result="denied"}
  3. Zipkin Trace: istio.authorization.dry_run.deny_policy.result: "denied"
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: test-deny-headers
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    istio.io/dry-run: "true"  # ← Shadow mode: evaluate but don't enforce
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: DENY
  rules:
  - to:
    - operation:
        paths: ["/admin"]    # Would block /admin... but only logs it!
⚠️ ICA Exam: Dry Run Limitations

1. Only works with ALLOW and DENY actions (not CUSTOM). 2. Both ALLOW and DENY dry-run results are logged separately — you must check BOTH. 3. Requires proxy debug logging: istioctl proxy-config log deploy/X --level rbac:debug. 4. Alpha feature — not for production API contracts. 5. To enforce: remove annotation or set to "false".

📝 Chapter 13 — ICA Practice Questions (Hands-On Lab Scenarios)

Q1
Build zero-trust for the anihpj namespace. Task: (a) Create a deny-all AuthorizationPolicy (empty spec = deny everything). (b) Verify by curling between services — all return 403. (c) Create an ALLOW policy: only jobpost-api's SPIFFE can GET /api/users/* on user-service. (d) Verify: jobpost-api → 200 OK, skills-service → 403. (e) Explain the evaluation order: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW.
Show Answer
Answer

Create an AuthorizationPolicy with an empty spec: spec: {}. With no rules, nothing is allowed → everything is denied. This is the starting point for zero-trust architecture.

Explanation

An empty spec means "no rules match" which means "nothing is allowed." This is the Istio zero-trust pattern: deny everything first, then create explicit ALLOW policies for specific call paths. On the ICA exam, this is the first step when building a zero-trust security model for a namespace.

Q2
You have deny-all applied. Now selectively allow traffic. Task: (a) ALLOW only jobpost-api (SPIFFE principal) to GET /api/users/* on user-service. (b) ALLOW only ingressgateway to call jobpost-api on GET /jobs/* and POST /jobs/. (c) Verify: unauthorized services get 403. (d) Explain: mTLS proves WHO (SPIFFE), AuthorizationPolicy controls WHAT (permissions). You need BOTH for zero-trust.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-jobpost-to-users, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: user-service}}
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET"]
        paths: ["/api/users/*"]

mTLS = identity verification. Authz = access control. Both needed for zero-trust.

Explanation

ALLOW rules combine who (SPIFFE principals) with what (HTTP methods + paths). Without both mTLS and Authz, you have identity without access control.

Q3
Write AuthorizationPolicies for all anihpj services. Task: (a) Deny-all for the namespace. (b) ALLOW ingressgateway → jobpost-api (GET /jobs/*, POST /jobs/). (c) ALLOW jobpost-api → user-service (GET /users/*). (d) ALLOW jobpost-api → skills-service (GET /skills/*). (e) ALLOW user-service → auth-service (POST /validate). Apply all and test each path — allowed paths → 200, denied paths → 403.
Show Answer
Answer
# Deny-all
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata: {name: deny-all, namespace: anihpj}
spec: {}
---
# Allow ingress → jobpost-api
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-ingress-to-jobpost, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}}
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/istio-ingressgateway-service-account"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
        paths: ["/jobs/*"]

Apply all, test each path, verify 200 for allowed, 403 for denied.

Explanation

Complete zero-trust microservices policy. Each service explicitly declares who can call what.

Q4
Test the default-deny behavior. Task: (a) With NO AuthorizationPolicy, curl between services → 200 (default allow-all). (b) Apply deny-all (empty spec). (c) Curl again → all 403. (d) Explain: the moment ANY policy targets a workload, default switches from ALLOW-ALL to DENY-ALL. Only explicitly ALLOWed traffic passes.
Show Answer
Answer

No policies = everything allowed. First policy applied = only what's explicitly ALLOWed passes. spec: {} with no rules = deny everything — the zero-trust starting point.

Explanation

This default-deny switch is the most important Authz concept for the ICA exam.

Q5
Use DENY policies to block a specific service. Task: (a) Create an ALLOW policy that allows ALL services in anihpj to call user-service. (b) Create a DENY policy blocking skills-service specifically. (c) Verify: jobpost-api → 200, skills-service → 403. (d) Explain: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW. DENY always beats ALLOW.
Show Answer
Answer
# DENY skills-service
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata: {name: deny-skills, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: user-service}}
  action: DENY
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/skills-service"]

DENY evaluated before ALLOW. Skills-service blocked even if an ALLOW policy would match.

Explanation

DENY carves exceptions from broad ALLOW. CUSTOM→DENY→ALLOW evaluation order.

Q6
Set up JWT authentication at the mesh level. Task: (a) Write a RequestAuthentication that validates JWTs from issuer auth.anihpj.com. (b) Write an AuthorizationPolicy that only allows requests with JWT claim role=admin to POST /jobs/. (c) Test: curl with valid admin JWT → 200. curl with user JWT → 403. curl without JWT → 401. Explain: RequestAuthentication validates tokens, AuthorizationPolicy enforces permissions.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata: {name: jwt-auth, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}}
  jwtRules:
  - issuer: "https://auth.anihpj.com"
    jwksUri: "https://auth.anihpj.com/.well-known/jwks.json"

RequestAuthentication = validates tokens (doesn't deny). AuthorizationPolicy = enforces based on claims. Both needed.

Explanation

RequestAuthentication is the bouncer checking IDs. AuthorizationPolicy is the guest list. Two separate CRDs, both required for JWT auth.

Q7
Combine SPIFFE + JWT for defense-in-depth. Task: Write an AuthorizationPolicy requiring BOTH: caller must be jobpost-api (SPIFFE) AND end-user JWT must have role=admin. Explain: even if attacker gets a SPIFFE cert, they still need a valid JWT. Two independent layers.
Show Answer
Answer
rules:
- from:
  - source:
      principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
  to:
  - operation:
      methods: ["POST"]
      paths: ["/api/jobs/*"]
  when:
  - key: request.auth.claims[role]
    values: ["admin"]

BOTH conditions: SPIFFE identity AND JWT role=admin. Defense-in-depth.

Explanation

Two-layer security: service identity (SPIFFE) + end-user identity (JWT). Both must pass.

Q8
Test DENY vs ALLOW priority. Task: (a) Create ALLOW for all anihpj services to user-service. (b) Create DENY for skills-service. (c) Curl from skills-service → 403 (DENY wins). (d) Curl from jobpost-api → 200 (ALLOW works). Verify evaluation order: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW.
Show Answer
Answer

DENY always beats ALLOW. Use DENY to blacklist specific callers from a broad ALLOW policy. Evaluation: CUSTOM→DENY→ALLOW.

Explanation

DENY policies are evaluated BEFORE ALLOW. Even if an ALLOW matches, a matching DENY blocks it.

Q9
Write a complete AuthorizationPolicy for user-service. Task: (a) Only jobpost-api can GET /api/users/*. (b) Only auth-service can POST /api/users/validate. (c) All other callers → 403. (d) All other methods/paths → 403. Apply and verify each rule with curl from the allowed and blocked services.
Show Answer
Answer
rules:
- from: [{source: {principals: [".../sa/jobpost-api"]}}]
  to: [{operation: {methods: ["GET"], paths: ["/api/users/*"]}}]
- from: [{source: {principals: [".../sa/auth-service"]}}]
  to: [{operation: {methods: ["POST"], paths: ["/api/users/validate"]}}]

Explicit least-privilege: only jobpost-api gets GET, only auth-service gets POST validate.

Explanation

Complete production AuthzPolicy — least privilege, specific callers per operation.

Q10
Comprehensive security drill. Task: (a) Apply STRICT mTLS (PeerAuthentication). (b) Apply deny-all Authz. (c) Create selective ALLOW policies for all 5 anihpj services. (d) Add JWT validation (RequestAuthentication). (e) Test all paths: allowed → 200, denied → 403, missing JWT → 401. (f) Verify in Kiali: green locks on all edges, graph shows allowed traffic only. (g) Explain the 3 security layers: mTLS→Authz→JWT.
Show Answer
Answer

Layer 1: mTLS (encryption + service identity). Layer 2: AuthorizationPolicy (service-level access control). Layer 3: RequestAuthentication+JWT (end-user identity). All three compose Istio's zero-trust security model.

Explanation

Complete security stack: encrypt everything (mTLS) → restrict services (Authz) → authenticate users (JWT).

📝 Part 7 Summary — Security (25% of ICA)

  • mTLS (Ch 12): Encrypts ALL service traffic. SPIFFE certs auto-issued, auto-rotated every 24h.
  • PeerAuthentication: PERMISSIVE (migration) → STRICT (enforce). Zero Django code changes.
  • AuthorizationPolicy (Ch 13): L7 firewall — allow/deny based on identity, method, path, headers.
  • RequestAuthentication: JWT validation at mesh level — no auth code in services.
  • Remember: mTLS = WHO (identity), AuthzPolicy = WHAT (permissions). You need BOTH.

Chapter 14: Canary Deployments — Safe Feature Releases

Deploying a new version is risky. Canary deployments let you send a small percentage of real users to v2, monitor it, and gradually ramp up — with instant rollback at any stage by changing one YAML value. No downtime, no DNS changes, no user impact.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🚀 Deployment 🎯 ICA 10%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Deploy v2 of jobpost-api using VirtualService weight-based canary (5%→25%→50%→100%)
  • ✅ Mirror 100% of production traffic to v2 for safe testing — responses are discarded
  • ✅ Rollback instantly (~2 seconds) by setting v2 weight to 0
  • ✅ Compare blue-green (instant 100% switch) vs canary (gradual ramp)
  • ✅ Monitor v1 vs v2 side-by-side in Kiali and Grafana Workload Dashboard
  • ✅ Set rollback thresholds: error rate > 2% above v1 OR p99 > 2× v1 = ROLLBACK
💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 14
  • "Deploy new version gradually" = VirtualService with weight-based routing to subset v2
  • "Test with production traffic safely" = VirtualService mirror to v2 (responses discarded!)
  • "Instant rollback" = Edit VS weight for v2 to 0 — ~2 seconds, no DNS/pod restart needed
  • "Monitor during canary" = Kiali (separate v1/v2 nodes) + Grafana Workload Dashboard
  • Rollback triggers: v2 error rate > 2% above v1, OR v2 p99 latency > 2× v1
  • Mirror vs Canary: Mirror = observe only (safe). Canary = real traffic (has risk). Use mirror FIRST.

14.1 The Full Canary Deployment Workflow

Phase-by-phase rollout for jobpost-api:v2 — from zero traffic to 100% production:

📈 CANARY LIFECYCLE — jobpost-api:v2 Gradual Rollout
Day 1
v1: 100% · v2: 0%
Deploy v2 only
Check v2 starts OK
Day 2
v1: 95% · v2: 5%
Error rate < 1%? ✅
Proceed
Day 3
v1: 75% · v2: 25%
p99 < 300ms? ✅
Proceed

v1: 50% · v2: 50%
v2 errors 5%? ⚠️
❌ ROLLBACK!
Day 7
v1: 0% · v2: 100%
Fix bug, restart
✅ Production!
💡 Instant Rollback

At ANY phase, rollback takes ~2 seconds: change weight to 0% for v2 in VirtualService. v1 handles all traffic instantly. User impact: ZERO. Compare this to a traditional deployment rollback which can take 10+ minutes.

📊 Deployment Strategy Comparison

StrategyTraffic SwitchRollback SpeedBest For
Canary (Istio)Gradual %~2sRisk mitigation, monitoring
Blue-GreenInstant 100%~2sFast switch, staging parity

14.2 Shadow / Mirror Traffic Testing

Mirror 100% of live traffic to v2 — but discard v2 responses. Users see v1, but v2 processes real production traffic silently. Best way to test under real load before going live.

yaml — Traffic Mirroring: v2 gets silent copy 

spec:
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v1              # Real users get v1
      weight: 100
    mirror:
      host: jobpost-api
      subset: v2                # v2 gets silent copy
    mirrorPercentage:
      value: 100.0              # Copy 100% to v2

# ✅ Users: 100% served by v1 (zero impact)
# ✅ v2: receives all real production requests
# ✅ Check v2 metrics BEFORE any user sees it

14.3 Blue-Green Deployments with Istio

Maintain two identical environments — blue (current) and green (new). Switch ALL traffic instantly with one YAML change. Rollback is equally instant.

🔵 BLUE (Current)

v1 running, 100% traffic. Green deployed but receives 0%. Both environments fully ready.

🟢 GREEN (New)

Switch: VS weight → v2:100%. Traffic cuts over instantly. If issues: switch back to blue — 2 seconds. No DNS propagation delay.

⚠️ ICA: Automated Rollback Criteria

On the exam, you MUST specify WHEN to rollback. Define thresholds BEFORE deployment: (a) Error rate: v2 > 2% above v1 → ROLLBACK. (b) Latency p99: v2 > 2× v1 → ROLLBACK. (c) Any 5xx from v2 that v1 doesn't have → ROLLBACK. Use Grafana/Kiali dashboards to monitor these in real-time.

Q1

(b) Verify v2 receives requests via Kiali (edge shows traffic). (c) Confirm v2 errors don't affect users — v1 responses are always returned. (d) Explain: mirrored responses are DISCARDED. Execute a full canary deployment for jobpost-api v2. Task: (a) Write VirtualService + DestinationRule with 95/5 split. (b) Verify in Kiali — v1/v2 show as separate nodes with traffic %. (c) Increase to 75/25, then 50/50, then 0/100. (d) At each step, monitor error rates and p99. (e) Explain: canary = gradual (safer), blue-green = instant 100% switch (faster). Both rollback in ~2s.

v2 error rate spikes to 8% during canary. Task: Rollback immediately: kubectl patch vs jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/http/0/route/1/weight","value":0}]'. Explain: ~2 seconds, zero user impact, no pod restart. Then investigate: check v2 logs, compare v1 vs v2 Grafana metrics, fix bug, retry from 5%. Thresholds: error >2% above v1 = rollback, p99 >2× v1 = rollback.

Answer

Rollback: set v2 weight to 0. ~2 seconds for Envoy to update. No DNS, no pod restart, no deployment revert. Traditional rollback: 5-10 minutes. Istio: 2 seconds.

Always rollback FIRST, debug SECOND. The 2-second rollback is Istio's killer feature for canary deployments.

(e) Deliberately crash v2 — users still get 200s from v1. (f) Restore v2. (g) Explain: mirror responses are DISCARDED, v2 failures never reach users.
Show Answer
Answer

Mirror = fire-and-forget. Even if v2 returns 500s or crashes, users always see v1's response. Mirror is for observation only.

Explanation

Mirroring is the safest testing method — zero blast radius. Use it before canary to verify v2 under real load.

Mirror: observe only (no risk). Canary: gradual rollout (low risk). Blue-Green: instant switch (high speed). Decision: risk level + environment parity needs.
